sources.title: OpenAI nears up to $30 billion funding round at $1.25 trillion valuation led by UAE investors - CNBC
passages: OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported.
OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.

The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential.
That valuation does not include new capital raised.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering.
In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation.
OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering .
Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person.
Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO.

The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said. Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public." Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported. passages: It also underscores that OpenAI has fallen behind Anthropic, which is targeting a $2 trillion valuation when it goes public next month.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has told his employees that now is not the right time for the company to go public, but it's still targeting an IPO in 2027.
The ChatGPT parent is about to raise $30 billion at a valuation of $1.25 trillion with investors from the United Arab Emirates and Coatue, an investment firm, leading the round.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

OpenAI had initially aimed for a $1.5 trillion valuation in the capital raise, and the lowered valuation could be another sign of fatigue in the AI sector, following the plunge in CoreWeave stock and Meta's sell-off after it reported negative free cash flow in its earnings report.
Discussions of a new funding round began in September when OpenAI was approached by investors.
Going public at the same time as Anthropic would be a mistake, and it makes sense for OpenAI to wait a few months for investors' appetites to rebuild for another blockbuster IPO.

The future of the AI sector ultimately hinges on the success of Anthropic and OpenAI, the two leading AI labs that are delivering the technology that has come to be known as "AI." Both of these companies will need to eventually be profitable in order for the valuations across the AI ecosystem and for OpenAI and Anthropic to make sense.
That money is being spent so businesses and consumers can use generative AI and related programs from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others.

sources.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
passages: OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg.
OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion.
Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety.

extraction.body: OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion. Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

extraction.body: OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering . The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said. Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public." Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported. The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans.

Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
The current figures fall well short of that target.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans.
There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

OpenAI just secured a massive bag, but it’s not what it expected. In a new funding round, OpenAI raises $11 billion to hit a valuation of $1.25 trillion. While it’s a jaw-dropping number, the deal values the ChatGPT maker lower than what the company was chasing only weeks ago.
The money landed on Friday, according to people familiar with the matter, as first reported here. And more could follow soon. So why does a trillion-dollar raise feel like a step back?

The $11 billion is only the opening tranche. The full round could reach about $20 billion, with the rest expected to close over the coming weeks. However, in late September, OpenAI was reportedly targeting $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation.

Both figures have since been dropped as the AI market faces some setbacks. As a result, roughly $10 billion in new capital and $150 billion have been shaved off OpenAI’s valuation. Still, the company remains up there, raising $122 billion at an $852 billion valuation in March this year.

Even after the cut, its value has jumped nearly 47% in about eight months. Few companies on earth can say that. Put simply, OpenAI is still growing fast. It’s just growing slower than its own ambitions.
More Updates: CesiumAstro Raises $730M To Launch New AI Satellites
The first tranche was reportedly led by Coatue Management and T. Rowe Price. SoftBank Group, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund, Andreessen Horowitz and a UAE investor group also joined in.
You’ll recognize most of those names. Many have backed OpenAI before. Their return tells you big money still believes in the long game, even at a lower price.

There’s another twist worth watching. OpenAI is said to be working with investment banks to open the round to high-net-worth and retail investors. If that happens, regular investors could grab a slice of a company that’s usually off-limits until it lists.
It comes down to market sentiment. AI stocks have taken a beating on public markets. Investors are asking tougher questions about whether massive infrastructure spending will actually pay off.
And since the US midterm elections, worries have grown about new hurdles for data center construction. Regulation is now on a lot of minds. OpenAI isn’t alone, either.

Rival Anthropic is reportedly feeling similar pressure, with potential IPO buyers eyeing a valuation well below its hopes. When two of AI’s biggest names both reset expectations, it says a lot about the wider market.
More Updates: Ethiopia Becomes Africa’s Fifth Largest Economy

Private valuations like these often hint at where public markets are heading. A trimmed target suggests investors now want proof, not just promises. Also, OpenAI pushed back its plans to go public, and a listing is now widely expected sometime in 2027.

This cash buys it time. Third, it’s a reality check for the whole AI trade. If you hold tech stocks, AI-themed funds, or even crypto tokens riding the AI narrative, sentiment around OpenAI ripples straight into your portfolio.

The bottom line? OpenAI can still raise money at a scale almost nobody else can match. But the era of valuations that only go up may be taking a breather. Watch how the remaining $9 billion lands. It could set the tone for AI investing heading into 2027.

sources.title: Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M
passages: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions. The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from Datadog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week. If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks. extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks Inc. (PANW) is negotiating to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli company that secures the digital credentials used by artificial intelligence agents, for roughly $500 million, according to people cited by The Information. The discussions are preliminary, and there is no assurance an agreement will be reached. If completed, the transaction would be the fifth acquisition the Santa Clara, California-based cybersecurity vendor has announced in 2026, as CEO Nikesh Arora pushes deeper into identity security and defenses built around autonomous AI systems. Clutch was founded in late 2023 by CEO Ofir Har-Chen, CTO Sagi Haas and R&D vice president Tal Kimhi. Its software tracks so-called non-human identities: the API keys, service accounts, tokens and passwords that let applications and automated tools talk to one another and reach corporate systems. As companies deploy AI agents that can read internal data and act on their own, the number of such credentials has multiplied, creating a new problem for security teams that must determine which agents have access, what they are allowed to do and whether their keys are being abused. The platform maps those identities across an organization's environment, flags excessive or exposed permissions, manages credentials through their lifecycle and detects suspicious use. Clutch has been extending the product to cover AI agents specifically. A purchase would build on Palo Alto's $25 billion takeover of CyberArk, completed in February 2026. CyberArk's business centers on controlling access for human employees, while Clutch addresses machine and agent credentials, making the two largely complementary rather than overlapping. Clutch has raised about $28.5 million in two disclosed rounds. Lightspeed Venture Partners led an $8.5 million seed round in July 2024, joined by Merlin Ventures and individual investors including Shlomo Kramer, Exabeam co-founder Nir Polak and HashiCorp co-founder Armon Dadgar. SignalFire led a $20 million Series A in January 2025, with Lightspeed and Merlin Ventures participating again. The company operates in Israel and the United States. At the reported price, a sale would be a sizable return for backers relative to capital raised, though Clutch's current valuation could not be determined and final terms remain unsettled. Palo Alto told The Information it does not discuss rumors or speculation. Clutch did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Palo Alto is scheduled to report results on Nov. 18. Analysts expect earnings of 97 cents a share, up from 93 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $3.31 billion versus $2.47 billion, according to consensus estimates cited in the coverage. The stock carries a consensus Buy rating and an average analyst price target of $414.17. Citigroup lifted its target to $440, and Wells Fargo raised its forecast to $525 in October. Shares trade at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 870, a premium that leaves little room for disappointment on growth. Note: Earnings and revenue figures are analyst consensus estimates ahead of the Nov. 18 report. The shares are widely held through cybersecurity and software funds. Palo Alto accounts for 9.02% of the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), 7.56% of the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) and 5.42% of the Amplify Cybersecurity ETF (HACK), so any re-rating tied to the deal or the earnings report would ripple through those products. For investors, the central question is whether Arora can keep paying up for tuck-in technology without straining a multiple already stretched by the CyberArk integration. Identity security has become one of the fastest-growing corners of the market as enterprises shift toward automated operations, and rivals including Microsoft and CrowdStrike are competing for the same budgets. A Clutch deal would be small relative to CyberArk, but it would signal that Palo Alto intends to own the agent-credential layer before larger competitors establish a foothold. sources.title: Palo Alto Networks Eyes $500M Clutch Buy in AI Security Arms Race
passages: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market.

With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations.

Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security.
If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks.

The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions.
The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities.
As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore.
Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces.

The talks come as enterprise security vendors scramble to address the security risks posed by autonomous AI systems now being deployed across corporate environments. Clutch was last valued at just $85 million, meaning Palo Alto is willing to pay nearly six times that figure to acquire the technology. The startup, backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire, has built a platform specifically designed to monitor and secure AI agents - the autonomous software systems that can take actions, access data, and make decisions without human oversight. As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore. Palo Alto Networks has been methodically building its AI security portfolio through a combination of internal development and strategic acquisitions. The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions. The valuation jump reflects both Clutch's technology and the broader market dynamics. Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security. Even Nvidia has entered the space, launching an open agent safety platform that provides full-stack governance for AI systems. For Palo Alto Networks, the acquisition would address a critical gap in its product lineup at a moment when customers are demanding comprehensive AI security solutions. The company competes directly with CrowdStrike, Fortinet, and other security vendors who are all racing to offer end-to-end protection for AI deployments. Losing ground in this emerging category could mean losing access to the next generation of enterprise security budgets. Lightspeed and SignalFire, Clutch's primary backers, stand to see substantial returns if the deal closes at the reported $500 million figure. Both firms have been active investors in the AI security space, betting early that protecting autonomous systems would become a major enterprise priority. The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities. Palo Alto Networks appears determined not to let that happen, even if it means paying a significant premium for a startup that was valued at a fraction of the purchase price just months ago. Early AI security concerns focused on model vulnerabilities, data poisoning, and prompt injection attacks. But as companies move from chatbots to autonomous agents that can access systems, move data, and take actions on behalf of users, the security model has to evolve. Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces. extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks Inc. (PANW) is negotiating to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli company that secures the digital credentials used by artificial intelligence agents, for roughly $500 million, according to people cited by The Information. The discussions are preliminary, and there is no assurance an agreement will be reached. If completed, the transaction would be the fifth acquisition the Santa Clara, California-based cybersecurity vendor has announced in 2026, as CEO Nikesh Arora pushes deeper into identity security and defenses built around autonomous AI systems. Clutch was founded in late 2023 by CEO Ofir Har-Chen, CTO Sagi Haas and R&D vice president Tal Kimhi. Its software tracks so-called non-human identities: the API keys, service accounts, tokens and passwords that let applications and automated tools talk to one another and reach corporate systems. As companies deploy AI agents that can read internal data and act on their own, the number of such credentials has multiplied, creating a new problem for security teams that must determine which agents have access, what they are allowed to do and whether their keys are being abused. The platform maps those identities across an organization's environment, flags excessive or exposed permissions, manages credentials through their lifecycle and detects suspicious use. Clutch has been extending the product to cover AI agents specifically. A purchase would build on Palo Alto's $25 billion takeover of CyberArk, completed in February 2026. CyberArk's business centers on controlling access for human employees, while Clutch addresses machine and agent credentials, making the two largely complementary rather than overlapping. Clutch has raised about $28.5 million in two disclosed rounds. Lightspeed Venture Partners led an $8.5 million seed round in July 2024, joined by Merlin Ventures and individual investors including Shlomo Kramer, Exabeam co-founder Nir Polak and HashiCorp co-founder Armon Dadgar. SignalFire led a $20 million Series A in January 2025, with Lightspeed and Merlin Ventures participating again. The company operates in Israel and the United States. At the reported price, a sale would be a sizable return for backers relative to capital raised, though Clutch's current valuation could not be determined and final terms remain unsettled. Palo Alto told The Information it does not discuss rumors or speculation. Clutch did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Palo Alto is scheduled to report results on Nov. 18. Analysts expect earnings of 97 cents a share, up from 93 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $3.31 billion versus $2.47 billion, according to consensus estimates cited in the coverage. The stock carries a consensus Buy rating and an average analyst price target of $414.17. Citigroup lifted its target to $440, and Wells Fargo raised its forecast to $525 in October. Shares trade at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 870, a premium that leaves little room for disappointment on growth. Note: Earnings and revenue figures are analyst consensus estimates ahead of the Nov. 18 report. The shares are widely held through cybersecurity and software funds. Palo Alto accounts for 9.02% of the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), 7.56% of the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) and 5.42% of the Amplify Cybersecurity ETF (HACK), so any re-rating tied to the deal or the earnings report would ripple through those products. For investors, the central question is whether Arora can keep paying up for tuck-in technology without straining a multiple already stretched by the CyberArk integration. Identity security has become one of the fastest-growing corners of the market as enterprises shift toward automated operations, and rivals including Microsoft and CrowdStrike are competing for the same budgets. A Clutch deal would be small relative to CyberArk, but it would signal that Palo Alto intends to own the agent-credential layer before larger competitors establish a foothold. sources.title: Palo Alto Networks Eyes $500M Clutch Buy in AI Security Arms Race
passages: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market.

With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations.

Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security.
If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks.

The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions.
The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities.
As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore.
Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter. The deal would value the young company at nearly six times its last funding round valuation of $85 million and marks the latest mega-acquisition in the exploding AI security market. If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks. Palo Alto Networks is closing in on a roughly $500 million deal to buy Clutch, a startup focused on securing AI agents, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiations. The talks come as enterprise security vendors scramble to address the security risks posed by autonomous AI systems now being deployed across corporate environments. Clutch was last valued at just $85 million, meaning Palo Alto is willing to pay nearly six times that figure to acquire the technology. The startup, backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire, has built a platform specifically designed to monitor and secure AI agents - the autonomous software systems that can take actions, access data, and make decisions without human oversight. As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore. The deal talks reveal how quickly AI agent security has transformed from a niche concern into a must-have capability for enterprise security platforms. Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market. Palo Alto Networks has been methodically building its AI security portfolio through a combination of internal development and strategic acquisitions. The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions. The valuation jump reflects both Clutch's technology and the broader market dynamics. Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security. Even Nvidia has entered the space, launching an open agent safety platform that provides full-stack governance for AI systems. For Palo Alto Networks, the acquisition would address a critical gap in its product lineup at a moment when customers are demanding comprehensive AI security solutions. The company competes directly with CrowdStrike, Fortinet, and other security vendors who are all racing to offer end-to-end protection for AI deployments. Losing ground in this emerging category could mean losing access to the next generation of enterprise security budgets. Lightspeed and SignalFire, Clutch's primary backers, stand to see substantial returns if the deal closes at the reported $500 million figure. Both firms have been active investors in the AI security space, betting early that protecting autonomous systems would become a major enterprise priority. The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities. The deal structure and timeline remain fluid, and there's no guarantee the talks will result in a completed transaction. But the momentum is clear: enterprise security is being rebuilt around AI, and the companies that can't secure autonomous agents risk becoming irrelevant. Palo Alto Networks appears determined not to let that happen, even if it means paying a significant premium for a startup that was valued at a fraction of the purchase price just months ago. Early AI security concerns focused on model vulnerabilities, data poisoning, and prompt injection attacks. But as companies move from chatbots to autonomous agents that can access systems, move data, and take actions on behalf of users, the security model has to evolve. Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces. Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Clutch at a 6x valuation premium signals that AI agent security has moved from emerging concern to existential priority for enterprise security vendors. With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations. As AI agents proliferate across corporate networks, expect more acquisitions, more funding rounds, and more competition for the startups building the guardrails that make autonomous AI safe for enterprise deployment.

Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security.
If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks.

The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions.
The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities.
As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore.
Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces.

sources.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
passages: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers.
Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent.
Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab.
Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it.
I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents.
Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week.
On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months.
During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The Tamagotchi-like gadget is designed for people who don't wear Meta's smart glasses, and Zuckerberg called it the fastest way to talk to Muse without wearing them. SEE ALSO: Meet the Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3, starting at $249 The reveal was set up earlier in the keynote. During a live demo, Zuckerberg used Meta's glasses to talk with his customized Muse assistant, which he'd named Agrippa, about a handheld device he was working on. That device turned out to be Muse Charm.Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Zuckerberg also suggested Meta could eventually collect a small fee on transactions the assistant helps complete.Muse Charm will ship by the holidays in December, according to Zuckerberg. Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later.The device enters a category with a rocky track record. Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year. Muse Charm's main selling point is that it runs on the same assistant as Meta's glasses.

extraction.body: Meta announced on November 6, 2026 that spaces are now available everywhere Muse is available, letting users create persistent, customized experiences inside the app by describing an idea and refining the result with Muse. Each space becomes a saved part of the app that can support routines, goals, interests, practical work, or entertainment. Meta’s introductory examples include a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, and a planning board for a do-it-yourself project, illustrating the range between organizational tools and lightweight interactive experiences. Creation begins with a description supplied to Muse . The initial result serves as a starting point: users can continue working with Muse to add missing elements, try a different appearance, or change how the space functions. This allows the experience to evolve as its purpose becomes clearer, while preserving it as something the user can revisit. Users also control how spaces fit into the broader interface. They can place them in the sidebar or main tabs, hide those they do not currently need, and schedule when particular spaces appear. One scheduling example keeps a weekly planner prominent during the workweek and then replaces it with weekend plans. The controls therefore cover both the contents of a space and its prominence within the app. The suggested uses extend across personal organization, entertainment, and business activity. A shopping hub can combine holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists drawn from Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, and buyer messages in one view. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually. Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices. Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services. Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives. Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals. Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation. Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine. Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models. coreStoryFacts.text: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers.
Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent.
Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab.
Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it.
I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents.
Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week.
On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months.
During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
Meta has added Spaces to Muse, its AI agent, allowing users to describe ideas in chat and have the agent build trackers, planners, or project boards.
Spaces can connect to third-party apps to stay automatically updated without manual intervention.
According to TechCrunch , Spaces are topic-focused conversations that sit in the sidebar of the Muse interface, where the agent works toward a specific goal for the user.
Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg posted on X that he had been using Spaces and had built a BBQ game, an event tracker and a home control dashboard.
"Tell Muse what you need and it builds it," he wrote.
Spaces arrives a day after Meta introduced Muse Voice, which lets users video chat with their agent and give it spoken commands.
TechCrunch reports that on Meta's October earnings call, Zuckerberg said Muse agents had reached 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada less than two months after launch.
TechCrunch names OpenAI's dots and SpaceXAI's Grokbot as competing agent products.
Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask. — Meta

extraction.body: Meta has a new way to talk to its AI without putting on a pair of glasses.At the end of Wednesday's Meta Connect keynote, CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Muse Charm, a small, always-on handheld device built around Muse, Meta's AI assistant. The Tamagotchi-like gadget is designed for people who don't wear Meta's smart glasses, and Zuckerberg called it the fastest way to talk to Muse without wearing them. SEE ALSO: Meet the Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3, starting at $249 The reveal was set up earlier in the keynote. During a live demo, Zuckerberg used Meta's glasses to talk with his customized Muse assistant, which he'd named Agrippa, about a handheld device he was working on. That device turned out to be Muse Charm.Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Zuckerberg also suggested Meta could eventually collect a small fee on transactions the assistant helps complete.Muse Charm will ship by the holidays in December, according to Zuckerberg. Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later.The device enters a category with a rocky track record. Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year. extraction.body: Meta announced on November 6, 2026 that spaces are now available everywhere Muse is available, letting users create persistent, customized experiences inside the app by describing an idea and refining the result with Muse. Each space becomes a saved part of the app that can support routines, goals, interests, practical work, or entertainment. Meta’s introductory examples include a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, and a planning board for a do-it-yourself project, illustrating the range between organizational tools and lightweight interactive experiences. Creation begins with a description supplied to Muse . The initial result serves as a starting point: users can continue working with Muse to add missing elements, try a different appearance, or change how the space functions. This allows the experience to evolve as its purpose becomes clearer, while preserving it as something the user can revisit. Users also control how spaces fit into the broader interface. They can place them in the sidebar or main tabs, hide those they do not currently need, and schedule when particular spaces appear. One scheduling example keeps a weekly planner prominent during the workweek and then replaces it with weekend plans. The controls therefore cover both the contents of a space and its prominence within the app. The suggested uses extend across personal organization, entertainment, and business activity. A shopping hub can combine holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists drawn from Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, and buyer messages in one view. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually. Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices. Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services. Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives. Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals. Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation. Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine. Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models. sources.title: Nothing’s first AI device will have no screen — and launches in December - Notebookcheck
passages: Nothing is preparing to launch its first AI-native device in December, and CEO Carl Pei says it will have no screen.
Pei has offered few details about the upcoming product, but describes it as a standalone tool rather than another AI-powered app.

Pei announced the launch in a post on X, describing the device as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.” He added that it “has no screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Nothing has not disclosed the product’s form, features, price, or exact launch date.
The only concrete detail is the absence of a display, alongside a teaser image showing the Nothing logo and an ambiguous black rounded corner.
The announcement comes a little over a year after Pei first outlined Nothing’s plans for AI-native devices and an AI operating system.
There have been rumors that Nothing is developing two pairs of AI smart glasses , one of which reportedly will not have cameras.
Screen-free AI devices are not entirely new, with products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend already attempting to bring AI assistants into standalone gadgets.

passages: The first Nothing AI device is set to ship as early as December 2026.
Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced this on November 4 in a lengthy essay titled “Toolmakers” on X.
There aren’t many details available yet beyond two key points: The device won’t feature a new screen, and, according to Pei, it couldn’t have been implemented as an app.
The name, price, specs, and a specific release date are still unknown.
Especially when it comes to data privacy for a device that’s supposed to be constantly listening, Nothing will have to explain very clearly in Europe where the recordings are processed.
Pei calls the device a tool, built with the personality and care that Nothing is known for.
Two details here are more interesting than they seem at first glance.
First, the word “new”: Pei doesn’t rule out that the device uses a screen—just not its own.
It stands to reason that your smartphone would take on this role, as Android Authority also points out.
Second, the word “ships”: Pei is talking about shipping, not just a December unveiling.
Whether this applies to Germany, however, remains to be seen.

There aren’t many details available yet beyond two key points: The device won’t feature a new screen, and, according to Pei, it couldn’t have been implemented as an app. The name, price, specs, and a specific release date are still unknown. The actual announcement comes at the very end of the essay, almost in passing. Pei calls the device a tool, built with the personality and care that Nothing is known for. The key sentence translates to: “It doesn’t have a new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Two details here are more interesting than they seem at first glance. First, the word “new”: Pei doesn’t rule out that the device uses a screen—just not its own. It stands to reason that your smartphone would take on this role, as Android Authority also points out. Second, the word “ships”: Pei is talking about shipping, not just a December unveiling. Whether this applies to Germany, however, remains to be seen. Most of the essay isn’t a product announcement, but rather a counterpoint to the industry. Pei takes a jab at the hunt for AI’s “iPhone moment”—that is, at the trackers, pins, glasses, and companion gadgets that many manufacturers are currently trying their luck with. He admires their courage but sees the situation differently. His argument goes like this: The iPhone was the culmination of decades of development, whereas AI is still in its infancy and stuck in the chat window. The models have long been powerful enough. What’s missing is context. Ideas from conversations and meetings rarely end up in writing anywhere, so AI knows little about your day. Nothing aims to close this “context gap.” Pei’s historical comparison fits well here: PCs and cell phones first gained traction in the workplace before making their way into living rooms. As an example, he cites the pager—which hung from the belts of doctors and anyone on call—as marking the beginning of mobile communication. sources.title: Nothing teases its first AI device with no screen, launching in December
passages: London-based tech brand Nothing, famous for its striking transparent smartphones and audio gear, is gearing up to launch its very first AI device this December.

More details are expected to be revealed in the coming weeks ahead of the December launch.Taking on Amazon and the AI hardware rushNothing's entry into the AI hardware space comes at a time when major tech companies are rushing to release their own AI gadgets ahead of the holiday season, including new Alexa tablets from Amazon, as well as AI-focused hardware from Apple and Microsoft.Specifically, Nothing's reportedly recorder will step into a market where Amazon is already expanding its presence with its own AI-based voice recorders.Following its acquisition of the San Francisco-based startup Bee in July 2025 for an undisclosed sum, Amazon recently unveiled two new AI-powered listening devices designed to record, transcribe, and analyse conversations.The first is the Bee Frontier, a $75 wearable that can be worn on the wrist or clipped directly to clothing.

By confirming a screenless design, it is evident that users will interact with the device primarily through voice or other non-visual methods.Instead of making a general smart gadget for the home, Nothing is aiming this device squarely at professionals to boost workplace productivity.

Nothing CEO Carl Pei recently took to X (formerly Twitter) to confirm the timeline, dropping some major hints about the upcoming gadget.Interestingly, this new "AI-native" product will completely ditch the display and is being built as a dedicated hardware tool, rather than just another smartphone application.A screenless gadget built for the workplaceWhile the official name, exact launch date, and pricing are still a closely guarded secret, Pei’s teasers give buyers a clear picture of the company's direction.

facts.text: Pei has teased an AI-first device for some time and the company has also said that it plans to release a pair of AI-linked smart glasses, as well as earbuds with AI integrations.

On Wednesday, CEO Carl Pei posted on X that the company’s first “AI-native product” ships in December. “It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.

Nothing is preparing to launch its first AI-native device in December, and CEO Carl Pei says it will have no screen.
Pei has offered few details about the upcoming product, but describes it as a standalone tool rather than another AI-powered app.

Pei announced the launch in a post on X, describing the device as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.” He added that it “has no screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Nothing has not disclosed the product’s form, features, price, or exact launch date.
The only concrete detail is the absence of a display, alongside a teaser image showing the Nothing logo and an ambiguous black rounded corner.
The announcement comes a little over a year after Pei first outlined Nothing’s plans for AI-native devices and an AI operating system.
There have been rumors that Nothing is developing two pairs of AI smart glasses , one of which reportedly will not have cameras.
Screen-free AI devices are not entirely new, with products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend already attempting to bring AI assistants into standalone gadgets.
The first Nothing AI device is set to ship as early as December 2026.
Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced this on November 4 in a lengthy essay titled “Toolmakers” on X.
There aren’t many details available yet beyond two key points: The device won’t feature a new screen, and, according to Pei, it couldn’t have been implemented as an app.
The name, price, specs, and a specific release date are still unknown.
Especially when it comes to data privacy for a device that’s supposed to be constantly listening, Nothing will have to explain very clearly in Europe where the recordings are processed.
Pei calls the device a tool, built with the personality and care that Nothing is known for.
Two details here are more interesting than they seem at first glance.
First, the word “new”: Pei doesn’t rule out that the device uses a screen—just not its own.
It stands to reason that your smartphone would take on this role, as Android Authority also points out.
Second, the word “ships”: Pei is talking about shipping, not just a December unveiling.
Whether this applies to Germany, however, remains to be seen.

OpenAI is working with Jony Ive on its own device without a traditional screen; according to Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon , several AI companies even plan to build their own smartphones; and in the smart glasses market, models like the XREAL Aura have long been driving change.
Nothing’s conclusion: first a productivity tool, then perhaps, at some point, the big consumer device.
London-based tech brand Nothing, famous for its striking transparent smartphones and audio gear, is gearing up to launch its very first AI device this December.

More details are expected to be revealed in the coming weeks ahead of the December launch.Taking on Amazon and the AI hardware rushNothing's entry into the AI hardware space comes at a time when major tech companies are rushing to release their own AI gadgets ahead of the holiday season, including new Alexa tablets from Amazon, as well as AI-focused hardware from Apple and Microsoft.Specifically, Nothing's reportedly recorder will step into a market where Amazon is already expanding its presence with its own AI-based voice recorders.Following its acquisition of the San Francisco-based startup Bee in July 2025 for an undisclosed sum, Amazon recently unveiled two new AI-powered listening devices designed to record, transcribe, and analyse conversations.The first is the Bee Frontier, a $75 wearable that can be worn on the wrist or clipped directly to clothing.

By confirming a screenless design, it is evident that users will interact with the device primarily through voice or other non-visual methods.Instead of making a general smart gadget for the home, Nothing is aiming this device squarely at professionals to boost workplace productivity.

extraction.body: The first Nothing AI device is set to ship as early as December 2026. Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced this on November 4 in a lengthy essay titled “Toolmakers” on X. There aren’t many details available yet beyond two key points: The device won’t feature a new screen, and, according to Pei, it couldn’t have been implemented as an app. The name, price, specs, and a specific release date are still unknown. The actual announcement comes at the very end of the essay, almost in passing. Pei calls the device a tool, built with the personality and care that Nothing is known for. The key sentence translates to: “It doesn’t have a new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Two details here are more interesting than they seem at first glance. First, the word “new”: Pei doesn’t rule out that the device uses a screen—just not its own. It stands to reason that your smartphone would take on this role, as Android Authority also points out. Second, the word “ships”: Pei is talking about shipping, not just a December unveiling. Whether this applies to Germany, however, remains to be seen. Most of the essay isn’t a product announcement, but rather a counterpoint to the industry. Pei takes a jab at the hunt for AI’s “iPhone moment”—that is, at the trackers, pins, glasses, and companion gadgets that many manufacturers are currently trying their luck with. He admires their courage but sees the situation differently. His argument goes like this: The iPhone was the culmination of decades of development, whereas AI is still in its infancy and stuck in the chat window. The models have long been powerful enough. What’s missing is context. Ideas from conversations and meetings rarely end up in writing anywhere, so AI knows little about your day. Nothing aims to close this “context gap.” Pei’s historical comparison fits well here: PCs and cell phones first gained traction in the workplace before making their way into living rooms. As an example, he cites the pager—which hung from the belts of doctors and anyone on call—as marking the beginning of mobile communication. Nothing’s conclusion: first a productivity tool, then perhaps, at some point, the big consumer device. Warning: this is where it gets speculative. Nothing hasn’t confirmed the form factor. However, the clues paint a fairly coherent picture: Anyone already familiar with Essential Space is currently using it on the Nothing Phone (3) , for example. A separate recording device that constantly listens in and provides context to the smartphone would be the logical hardware extension. Pei had already announced an AI-native device back in September 2025. At that time, Nothing raised $200 million in a Series C funding round led by Tiger Global, at a valuation of $1.3 billion. The first device was promised for 2026. Nothing is now just barely on track to meet that timeline. The road hasn’t been easy. This summer, Nothing confirmed a workforce reduction of about 40 percent while establishing its own “AI-native” business unit. At the same time, skyrocketing memory prices are taking a toll on affordable smartphones like the Nothing Phone (4b) . The AI device is therefore also a bet that Nothing won’t rely solely on the smartphone business in the future. The competition isn’t standing still. OpenAI is working with Jony Ive on its own device without a traditional screen; according to Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon , several AI companies even plan to build their own smartphones; and in the smart glasses market, models like the XREAL Aura have long been driving change. At the same time, the Humane Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 demonstrate just how quickly screenless AI gadgets can fail if they lack practical everyday utility. With “Toolmakers,” Pei skillfully steers clear of the hype trap. If you don’t promise an “AI iPhone,” you can’t fail by not delivering one. That’s a smart move in the wake of Humane’s disaster, and the lack of context is a real problem: Anyone who’s ever tried in vain to piece together the key points from memory after a meeting will immediately understand what Pei is getting at. My concern is different. If the Nothing AI device turns out to be nothing more than a stylishly designed voice recorder, Nothing will be entering a market that Plaud and others already occupy quite well. Then it won’t be the vision that matters, but rather, quite simply: price, transcription quality, data privacy, and whether the device works seamlessly with smartphones from other manufacturers. Especially when it comes to data privacy for a device that’s supposed to be constantly listening, Nothing will have to explain very clearly in Europe where the recordings are processed. We’ll know more in December. Basic Tutorials is a gaming and tech blog that keeps you up to date with in-depth news, reviews, tutorials and the latest deals from the world of gaming and technology. sources.title: Nothing teases its first AI device with no screen, launching in December
passages: London-based tech brand Nothing, famous for its striking transparent smartphones and audio gear, is gearing up to launch its very first AI device this December.

If you decide not to bother, the thought is usually forgotten by the end of the day.To solve this, reports strongly suggest that Nothing's product could be an ambient voice recorder that seamlessly captures these moments without interrupting your flow. Up from the $50 price tag of its earlier version, the new Frontier offers a seven-day battery life and upgraded noise-filtering technology across its dual microphones.This allows the device to clearly pick up important conversations while blocking out background chatter in busy restaurants or open-plan offices.Alongside the immediately available Frontier wearable, Amazon also introduced the $100 Bee Eclipse. Expected to go on sale soon, this device is not meant to be worn. Instead, it is a credit card-sized voice recorder that snaps magnetically to the back of a smartphone, offering similar AI-powered listening features.When Nothing finally unveils its new gadget this December, it will have to compete directly with these established AI wearables and personal recording devices.- EndsAlso Read | Exclusive: As Nothing completes one year, brand now gearing to launch over 5 new productsAlso Read | Amazon launches AI wearables that can listen in on your conversations and remember everythingAlso Read | Delhi Police registers FIR against Meta India over child sexual abuse content

extraction.body: China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says. Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new. The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

Alice Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, isn't related to Jensen Huang.Who is Alice Huang?According to a 2025 New York Times report, Alice Huang has a scant online profile, but she has spent much of her career in China, which included working as a television reporter for Chinese state media.

Alice has reportedly also described herself as the firm's chief executive.What is she accused of?Citing people familiar with the matter, WSJ reported that authorities in Singapore, where Megaspeed is headquartered, and Taiwan have conducted separate investigations into Alice's China connections and deployed teams to monitor her movements.

With Huang's encouragement, Trump has reportedly enacted industry-friendly chip and AI policies, along with approving some sales of previous Nvidia chips to Beijing while negotiating with his counterpart Xi Jinping.In late 2024, officials from the US Commerce Department started investigating whether the Singapore-based Megaspeed was involved in diverting Nvidia's chips to China, bypassing Washington's export controls meant to protect crucial technologies.US security experts have raised concerns that companies may be bypassing restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips by setting up data centres in neighbouring countries and offering Chinese businesses remote access to their computing power.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's reportedly close ties to a data-centre industry executive have now become a growing concern for officials in the US, Singapore and Taiwan. The executive is believed to be a Chinese intelligence source, possibly giving Beijing access to information about the world's most valuable artificial intelligence (AI) chips.According to The Wall Street Journal, in 2025, US officials concluded that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and top executive at Megaspeed International, passed information to the Chinese government while working with chipmaker Nvidia to build data centres in Asia. Alice Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, isn't related to Jensen Huang.Who is Alice Huang?According to a 2025 New York Times report, Alice Huang has a scant online profile, but she has spent much of her career in China, which included working as a television reporter for Chinese state media. According to a biography found on the social media of one of her former employers, she also worked as a private banker.She was also listed as a managing director for Megaspeed for its first eight months before she was removed from that role in its corporate paperwork. Alice has reportedly also described herself as the firm's chief executive.What is she accused of?Citing people familiar with the matter, WSJ reported that authorities in Singapore, where Megaspeed is headquartered, and Taiwan have conducted separate investigations into Alice's China connections and deployed teams to monitor her movements. Officials involved in the investigations suspected that Alice was recruited by intelligence agencies in Beijing after becoming aware of what they considered a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief.However, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs clarified on 31 October that neither the government nor its officials had expressed the concerns attributed to them in the WSJ report, and that no such investigations into Alice Huang’s alleged ties to Chinese intelligence had been conducted. It separately confirmed that investigations into Megaspeed were ongoing. In late 2024, when authorities began surveillance on Alice, she reportedly disappeared into Beijing for a while. Further, it can't be confirmed where she is now or whether she still holds a top executive role at Megaspeed.Chinese Embassy in US rejects allegationsWSJ reported that the Chinese Embassy in Washington rejected the allegations, saying that Beijing opposes what it described as the peddling of a "Chinese spy narrative" and adding that the country's technological development is grounded in "independent innovation."An Nvidia spokesperson said, "We’re confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," and added that CEO Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice "are not unusual or unexpected” given their business ties.A representative of the Singapore Police Force said investigations into Megaspeed were ongoing and declined to give specifics. “While we do not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, we act firmly against companies and individuals who violate our laws and are engaged in fraudulent and dishonest practices,” the representative said.Megaspeed probe and concerns over AI chip export loopholesChipmaker Nvidia's technology is said to be one of the most valued American technology assets, making its CEO a global superstar and helping him establish a close relationship with US President Donald Trump. With Huang's encouragement, Trump has reportedly enacted industry-friendly chip and AI policies, along with approving some sales of previous Nvidia chips to Beijing while negotiating with his counterpart Xi Jinping.In late 2024, officials from the US Commerce Department started investigating whether the Singapore-based Megaspeed was involved in diverting Nvidia's chips to China, bypassing Washington's export controls meant to protect crucial technologies.US security experts have raised concerns that companies may be bypassing restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips by setting up data centres in neighbouring countries and offering Chinese businesses remote access to their computing power. Analysts have also criticised the Trump administration for what they see as a reluctance to address these regulatory gaps.

sources.title: Spy targeting Nvidia CEO was alleged China intelligence service recruit: Report
passages: Washington DC: The Chinese businesswoman, with whom Nvidia's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Jensen Huang had alleged ties, was recruited as a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported, citing a memo circulated among policymakers in the Trump administration.On Friday, three House Republican committee chairs have asked Nvidia CEO to address, behind closed doors, the reported links with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of providing information to Beijing, Axios reported.Nvidia has denied the allegations as baseless .A top executive at a Singapore-based data centre firm named Megaspeed faced intense scrutiny over potential involvement in diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips towards China, as outlined in a report by The New York Times.

He also finalised a deal with Trump permitting the US government to secure a 25 per cent stake in specific Nvidia processors authorised for sale to China.As the Trump administration considered a comprehensive ban on Nvidia chip exports to China, Huang and his spouse travelled to Mar-a-Lago to persuade Trump to allow technology firms to continue doing business with Beijing.
As per the report, the Nvidia chief executive successfully lobbied the administration during Trump's second term to reverse stricter export controls governing the company's chip shipments to China.
I've always found Jensen Huang to be very aboveboard.
