extraction.body: A senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed was under scrutiny over suspicions that she had helped divert advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. Now, according to a report by The New York Times, American intelligence officials have concluded that she was possibly a Chinese intelligence asset, passing information to Beijing. The investigation also revealed that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive. For years, Washington has sought to restrict China's access to the technology and expertise needed to match or surpass the United States in the intensifying global race for AI dominance. The possibility that Beijing may have gained information through someone with close ties to Jensen Huang, a central figure in the AI industry and an ally of US President Donald Trump, could raise further concerns in Washington. According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings, which had not previously been reported, but chose not to act. The report further states that American officials had already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade restrictions on its access to advanced AI chips. However, the assessment that she may have been passing information directly to Beijing has raised additional concerns. The situation is further complicated by Jensen Huang's reported access to Trump's thinking on an issue of critical importance to both countries, particularly as the US president prepares to visit China next month. Megaspeed said its “current leadership” was taking the matter “extremely seriously” and was committed to establishing the facts behind the allegations. Alice Huang's background Reporting by The New York Times has traced Alice Huang's rise from a Chinese businesswoman and investor to a senior executive at Megaspeed, a company that the US Commerce Department had begun scrutinising over suspicions that it was helping China evade American export restrictions and gain access to Nvidia's computing power. The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site suspicious. Nvidia equipment was still in its delivery packaging, raising concerns that the hardware might have been intended for onward shipment rather than installation at the facility. The US government has restricted exports of its most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022. While some firms have allegedly smuggled chips across the Chinese border, others have legally established businesses in Southeast Asia that purchase large quantities of chips to build data centres serving Chinese companies. Megaspeed has effectively operated as an intermediary, purchasing Nvidia chips through the American arm of Inspur. The parent company of Inspur had been blacklisted by the US government over allegations of supplying technology to the Chinese military. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia has also reportedly purchased advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between 2024 and February 2026. Nvidia is known to evaluate customers before selling them its chips and technology. Megaspeed has continued to appear on Nvidia's website, while a job advertisement from Megaspeed's Indonesian branch described the company as a “premier business partner of Nvidia”. Further questions have been raised about Alice Huang's background. She has maintained a limited public profile on the Chinese internet and has at times described herself as Megaspeed's chief executive, while the company has listed her as its managing director. She subsequently worked with several financial firms, including Hexi Capital. Media reports have also raised questions about how Megaspeed's executive used her connections to secure funding, promote the company's rapidly expanding network of businesses, pitch new projects, recruit employees and launch other initiatives. Megaspeed is also moving ahead with the construction of a major data centre in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new AI facilities have emerged amid palm oil plantations. The company has already secured the chips required for the project, adding another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding its access to advanced Nvidia hardware.

Now, according to a report by The New York Times, American intelligence officials have concluded that she was possibly a Chinese intelligence asset, passing information to Beijing. The investigation also revealed that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive. For years, Washington has sought to restrict China's access to the technology and expertise needed to match or surpass the United States in the intensifying global race for AI dominance. The possibility that Beijing may have gained information through someone with close ties to Jensen Huang, a central figure in the AI industry and an ally of US President Donald Trump, could raise further concerns in Washington. According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings, which had not previously been reported, but chose not to act. The report further states that American officials had already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade restrictions on its access to advanced AI chips. However, the assessment that she may have been passing information directly to Beijing has raised additional concerns. The situation is further complicated by Jensen Huang's reported access to Trump's thinking on an issue of critical importance to both countries, particularly as the US president prepares to visit China next month. Megaspeed said its “current leadership” was taking the matter “extremely seriously” and was committed to establishing the facts behind the allegations. Alice Huang's background Reporting by The New York Times has traced Alice Huang's rise from a Chinese businesswoman and investor to a senior executive at Megaspeed, a company that the US Commerce Department had begun scrutinising over suspicions that it was helping China evade American export restrictions and gain access to Nvidia's computing power. The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site suspicious. Nvidia equipment was still in its delivery packaging, raising concerns that the hardware might have been intended for onward shipment rather than installation at the facility. The US government has restricted exports of its most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022. While some firms have allegedly smuggled chips across the Chinese border, others have legally established businesses in Southeast Asia that purchase large quantities of chips to build data centres serving Chinese companies. Megaspeed has effectively operated as an intermediary, purchasing Nvidia chips through the American arm of Inspur. The parent company of Inspur had been blacklisted by the US government over allegations of supplying technology to the Chinese military. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia has also reportedly purchased advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between 2024 and February 2026. Nvidia is known to evaluate customers before selling them its chips and technology. Megaspeed has continued to appear on Nvidia's website, while a job advertisement from Megaspeed's Indonesian branch described the company as a “premier business partner of Nvidia”. Further questions have been raised about Alice Huang's background. She has maintained a limited public profile on the Chinese internet and has at times described herself as Megaspeed's chief executive, while the company has listed her as its managing director. She subsequently worked with several financial firms, including Hexi Capital. Media reports have also raised questions about how Megaspeed's executive used her connections to secure funding, promote the company's rapidly expanding network of businesses, pitch new projects, recruit employees and launch other initiatives. Megaspeed is also moving ahead with the construction of a major data centre in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new AI facilities have emerged amid palm oil plantations. The company has already secured the chips required for the project, adding another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding its access to advanced Nvidia hardware.

According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings, which had not previously been reported, but chose not to act.
The report further states that American officials had already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade restrictions on its access to advanced AI chips.
However, the assessment that she may have been passing information directly to Beijing has raised additional concerns.

The situation is further complicated by Jensen Huang's reported access to Trump's thinking on an issue of critical importance to both countries, particularly as the US president prepares to visit China next month.
Megaspeed said its “current leadership” was taking the matter “extremely seriously” and was committed to establishing the facts behind the allegations.

Alice Huang's background Reporting by The New York Times has traced Alice Huang's rise from a Chinese businesswoman and investor to a senior executive at Megaspeed, a company that the US Commerce Department had begun scrutinising over suspicions that it was helping China evade American export restrictions and gain access to Nvidia's computing power.
The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site suspicious.
Nvidia equipment was still in its delivery packaging, raising concerns that the hardware might have been intended for onward shipment rather than installation at the facility.
The US government has restricted exports of its most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022.

While some firms have allegedly smuggled chips across the Chinese border, others have legally established businesses in Southeast Asia that purchase large quantities of chips to build data centres serving Chinese companies.
Megaspeed has effectively operated as an intermediary, purchasing Nvidia chips through the American arm of Inspur.
The parent company of Inspur had been blacklisted by the US government over allegations of supplying technology to the Chinese military.
Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia has also reportedly purchased advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between 2024 and February 2026.
Nvidia is known to evaluate customers before selling them its chips and technology.
Megaspeed has continued to appear on Nvidia's website, while a job advertisement from Megaspeed's Indonesian branch described the company as a “premier business partner of Nvidia”.
Further questions have been raised about Alice Huang's background.
She has maintained a limited public profile on the Chinese internet and has at times described herself as Megaspeed's chief executive, while the company has listed her as its managing director.
She subsequently worked with several financial firms, including Hexi Capital.

Media reports have also raised questions about how Megaspeed's executive used her connections to secure funding, promote the company's rapidly expanding network of businesses, pitch new projects, recruit employees and launch other initiatives.

Megaspeed is also moving ahead with the construction of a major data centre in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new AI facilities have emerged amid palm oil plantations.
The company has already secured the chips required for the project, adding another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding its access to advanced Nvidia hardware.

ADRs of TSMC surged 7.7% in early trading Friday as investors weighed the prospect of the foundry giant deepening its role in the critical AI hardware supply chain.

The Taiwanese manufacturer recently began formulating plans to produce vertically stacked 3D DRAM at the behest of its primary customer, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter cited by The Information.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The company's exploration is being spearheaded by Hsu Kuo-chin, a vice president directing TSMC's advanced packaging operations who previously ran Micron's regional footprint.

His oversight underscores how intimately memory architecture has become linked with advanced packaging, the specialized process required to tether memory and processing units into cohesive computing systems.
TSMC is examining whether to construct dedicated fabrication facilities or acquire and retool an existing site to support the specialized production, the report indicated.

That latter path mirrors a maneuver by Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU), which in March agreed to purchase a Taiwan-based facility from Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. for $1.8 billion to retrofit for high-end memory.
A persistent bottleneck in memory availability has driven hardware costs sharply higher, prompting key buyers such as Nvidia and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) to actively seek alternative procurement channels.
Apple, for its part, implemented price increases across its hardware portfolio earlier this year after absorbing substantial increases in memory procurement expenses.
Entering the memory arena would nonetheless expose TSMC to a notoriously volatile segment long dominated by Samsung Electronics (KS:005930), SK hynix Inc (NASDAQ:SKHY), and Micron.

Memory markets are historically prone to severe boom-and-bust supply imbalances, and while TSMC holds proprietary patents around vertical DRAM, translating lab designs into defect-free volume manufacturing poses formidable execution hurdles.

The strategic shift also introduces delicate competitive dynamics, particularly following TSMC's 2024 pact to manufacture base logic dies for SK Hynix's next-generation high-bandwidth memory products.

coreStoryFacts.text: TSMC rises on report of potential push into advanced memory for Nvidia
ADRs of TSMC surged 7.7% in early trading Friday as investors weighed the prospect of the foundry giant deepening its role in the critical AI hardware supply chain.

The Taiwanese manufacturer recently began formulating plans to produce vertically stacked 3D DRAM at the behest of its primary customer, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter cited by The Information.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The company's exploration is being spearheaded by Hsu Kuo-chin, a vice president directing TSMC's advanced packaging operations who previously ran Micron's regional footprint.

His oversight underscores how intimately memory architecture has become linked with advanced packaging, the specialized process required to tether memory and processing units into cohesive computing systems.
TSMC is examining whether to construct dedicated fabrication facilities or acquire and retool an existing site to support the specialized production, the report indicated.

That latter path mirrors a maneuver by Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU), which in March agreed to purchase a Taiwan-based facility from Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. for $1.8 billion to retrofit for high-end memory.
A persistent bottleneck in memory availability has driven hardware costs sharply higher, prompting key buyers such as Nvidia and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) to actively seek alternative procurement channels.
Apple, for its part, implemented price increases across its hardware portfolio earlier this year after absorbing substantial increases in memory procurement expenses.
Entering the memory arena would nonetheless expose TSMC to a notoriously volatile segment long dominated by Samsung Electronics (KS:005930), SK hynix Inc (NASDAQ:SKHY), and Micron.

Memory markets are historically prone to severe boom-and-bust supply imbalances, and while TSMC holds proprietary patents around vertical DRAM, translating lab designs into defect-free volume manufacturing poses formidable execution hurdles.

The strategic shift also introduces delicate competitive dynamics, particularly following TSMC's 2024 pact to manufacture base logic dies for SK Hynix's next-generation high-bandwidth memory products.
According to a report from The Information, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is considering a push into advanced memory chips, with internal plans focused on 3D DRAM .
The report ties the effort to demand from Nvidia , TSMC’s largest client.
The key word throughout is “considering.” TSMC is described as formulating plans, not breaking ground on memory fabs.
No timeline, investment figure, or production target appears in the reporting.
That was still enough to move Micron and SK Hynix, which says a lot about how jittery the AI supply chain has become.
TSMC, the company that builds the brains of the AI boom, is reportedly thinking about building its memory too.
TSMC built its reputation as a logic foundry.
It manufactures processors designed by other companies, rather than selling its own branded chips.
The research also raises a second path: partnerships with existing memory specialists.
That route would let TSMC expand its footprint without building an entire memory operation from scratch.
For AI chip buyers, including Nvidia, the stakes look different.

passages: Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday.
Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing.
The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to.
Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov.

passages: Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

passages: Nvidia has pushed back after chief executive Jensen Huang was asked to appear before the US Congress to discuss his interactions with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

A representative for the powerful US-based AI and chip design company did not say whether Mr Huang would agree to attend the meeting with members of Congress, who requested his presence following reports that the Nvidia boss met with an executive of a Singapore company who is believed to have passed along information to China.

Republican Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Eric Crawford told the Nvidia boss in the letter that they have long been concerned about alleged Chinese espionage and the potential for it to result in the country getting access to “cutting-edge US technology”.
The House of Representatives select committee on the Chinese Communist Party had sent a letter to Mr Huang to request that he appear for a closed-door briefing.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security,” the Nvidia representative said.

Many Democrats across the country campaigned on trying to hold Big Tech executives more accountable, pushing for AI regulation and casting a critical eye on data centres – and all this might be bad news for Nvidia and Mr Huang.
Nvidia's push for relaxed export policies to China with regard to semiconductors has led to increased scrutiny in recent years.

On Wednesday, Mr Blumenthal issued a notice to people, companies and government agencies that have “failed to co-operate” with a range of inquiries, including investigations into Big Tech and cryptocurrency. Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who will soon be in charge of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, was a bit more succinct following the midterms.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

Republican Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Eric Crawford told the Nvidia boss in the letter that they have long been concerned about alleged Chinese espionage and the potential for it to result in the country getting access to “cutting-edge US technology”.
The House of Representatives select committee on the Chinese Communist Party had sent a letter to Mr Huang to request that he appear for a closed-door briefing.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security,” the Nvidia representative said.

Many Democrats across the country campaigned on trying to hold Big Tech executives more accountable, pushing for AI regulation and casting a critical eye on data centres – and all this might be bad news for Nvidia and Mr Huang.
Nvidia's push for relaxed export policies to China with regard to semiconductors has led to increased scrutiny in recent years.

extraction.body: Nvidia has pushed back after chief executive Jensen Huang was asked to appear before the US Congress to discuss his interactions with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. A representative for the powerful US-based AI and chip design company did not say whether Mr Huang would agree to attend the meeting with members of Congress, who requested his presence following reports that the Nvidia boss met with an executive of a Singapore company who is believed to have passed along information to China. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security,” the Nvidia representative said. The House of Representatives select committee on the Chinese Communist Party had sent a letter to Mr Huang to request that he appear for a closed-door briefing. Republican Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Eric Crawford told the Nvidia boss in the letter that they have long been concerned about alleged Chinese espionage and the potential for it to result in the country getting access to “cutting-edge US technology”. “Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the letter concluded, asking for Mr Huang to appear and discuss his interactions with the alleged Chinese asset on November 18 behind closed doors. The Nvidia representative told The National that the company has a robust security team that travels with its chief executive “when needed”, and that the company always acts accordingly when it receives updates from the US government about entities of concern. “We're confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the representative added. Mr Huang has become a familiar face in the halls of power in Washington over the past year, as he lobbied officials on US technology export policies. Nvidia's push for relaxed export policies to China with regard to semiconductors has led to increased scrutiny in recent years. Company executives have insisted that strict export policies designed to improve the US lead over China in AI actually hurt the country and incentivise Beijing to use its own technology and develop in-house infrastructure. Critics say that by loosening export restrictions, the US is giving away its most important advantage to an adversary. The letter to Mr Huang was sent a day after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. Many Democrats across the country campaigned on trying to hold Big Tech executives more accountable, pushing for AI regulation and casting a critical eye on data centres – and all this might be bad news for Nvidia and Mr Huang. On Wednesday, Mr Blumenthal issued a notice to people, companies and government agencies that have “failed to co-operate” with a range of inquiries, including investigations into Big Tech and cryptocurrency. The notice said failure to produce requested records and information by January 4 would lead the committee to consider “alternative measures”. “Blumenthal is leading an inquiry into Big Tech companies and others who may be seeking pay-to-play government favours from their donations to President Trump’s White House ballroom and other projects,” a news release from Mr Blumenthal's office read. Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who will soon be in charge of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, was a bit more succinct following the midterms.

Wall Street appears to have found a silver lining following the Democrats' sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections. With Democrats gaining control of both chambers of Congress , investors are considering whether more regulation could slow the construction of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across the United States. At first glance, that might actually benefit Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG), and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). After all, building AI infrastructure is expensive. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » If Big Tech is forced to reduce capital expenditures (capex), their free cash flow could improve. Meanwhile, a shortage of compute capacity could allow existing data center operators to charge higher prices. While this all makes sense in theory, I think Wall Street may be overlooking an important possibility. Over the last several years, the hyperscalers have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to expanding AI infrastructure. These investments include procuring graphics processing units (GPUs), building data centers, and securing electricity. However, a number of candidates used data centers as a controversial topic during their time on the campaign trail. For many people around the country, data centers have fueled rising utility costs. Following the midterms, Wall Street is considering whether new legislation or tighter permitting requirements could make additional U.S. data center projects more difficult to pursue. The financial argument is pretty straightforward: If the hyperscalers slow down their infrastructure investments, capex would decline and free cash flow would rise. At the same time, continued demand for compute could create a supply demand imbalance. Companies with existing capacity would be in a position to charge higher utilization and command pricing power. The combination of lower spending and higher revenue per unit of compute would be favorable for the hyperscalers. With that said, this assumes that AI developers respond to potential regulatory restrictions by slowing down the pace of their infrastructure roadmaps. During a discussion with The Wall Street Journal on Nov. 4, Meta's president and vice chair, Dina Powell McCormick, acknowledged that the election results could complicate future data center development domestically. She says starting new domestic projects may be harder and raised a question that could reshape the AI investment narrative: "Do we need to build outside the United States?" There's already evidence that Big Tech is willing to invest internationally. Consider some of their existing projects: More than $10 billion is planned across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait through 2030. More than $5 billion is planned in Mexico over 15 years. A $15 billion AI infrastructure investment planned for Visakhapatnam, India between 2026 and 2030. 13 billion Canadian dollars for a 1-gigawatt AI data center in Alberta, plus a 168-megawatt AI data center lease agreement in Jamnagar, India. Data source: Company press releases, Wall Street Journal , Reuters. These investments were announced before the midterms, so they shouldn't be interpreted as reactions to the election. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that hyperscalers already have international infrastructure strategies in place. If new restrictions make projects in certain states less attractive, I wouldn't be surprised to see Big Tech evaluate opportunities elsewhere and accelerate overseas development. Suppose new federal or state regulations delay data center construction in the U.S. Initially, the hyperscalers may postpone their projects, causing capex to decline and free cash flow to improve. In turn, investors may cheer these tighter cost controls and higher profits, leading to rising stock prices. Still, I question whether the hyperscalers would willingly delay expansion plans for two years while waiting for the 2028 presidential election. That strategy introduces another layer of uncertainty without guaranteeing a more favorable regulatory environment afterward. Most importantly, redirecting AI infrastructure investments overseas would not generate the sustained improvements to cash flow Wall Street is anticipating. The hyperscalers could easily continue pouring hundreds of billions of dollars annually on AI infrastructure, just in different countries. Ultimately, I think investors need to distinguish between a slowdown in U.S. data center construction and a slowdown in global AI investment. Those are two different outcomes. For now, Wall Street seems interested in the possibility that tighter regulation could improve Big Tech's financial performance in the near term. If hyperscalers respond by expanding internationally, the anticipated cash flow windfall could prove much smaller than expected. The combination of lower spending and higher revenue per unit of compute would be favorable for the hyperscalers. With that said, this assumes that AI developers respond to potential regulatory restrictions by slowing down the pace of their infrastructure roadmaps.

During a discussion with The Wall Street Journal on Nov. 4, Meta's president and vice chair, Dina Powell McCormick, acknowledged that the election results could complicate future data center development domestically. She says starting new domestic projects may be harder and raised a question that could reshape the AI investment narrative: "Do we need to build outside the United States?"
There's already evidence that Big Tech is willing to invest internationally. Consider some of their existing projects:
Data source: Company press releases, Wall Street Journal , Reuters.

These investments were announced before the midterms, so they shouldn't be interpreted as reactions to the election. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that hyperscalers already have international infrastructure strategies in place. If new restrictions make projects in certain states less attractive, I wouldn't be surprised to see Big Tech evaluate opportunities elsewhere and accelerate overseas development.

Suppose new federal or state regulations delay data center construction in the U.S. Initially, the hyperscalers may postpone their projects, causing capex to decline and free cash flow to improve. In turn, investors may cheer these tighter cost controls and higher profits, leading to rising stock prices.

Still, I question whether the hyperscalers would willingly delay expansion plans for two years while waiting for the 2028 presidential election. That strategy introduces another layer of uncertainty without guaranteeing a more favorable regulatory environment afterward.

Most importantly, redirecting AI infrastructure investments overseas would not generate the sustained improvements to cash flow Wall Street is anticipating. The hyperscalers could easily continue pouring hundreds of billions of dollars annually on AI infrastructure, just in different countries.
Ultimately, I think investors need to distinguish between a slowdown in U.S. data center construction and a slowdown in global AI investment. Those are two different outcomes.

For now, Wall Street seems interested in the possibility that tighter regulation could improve Big Tech's financial performance in the near term. If hyperscalers respond by expanding internationally, the anticipated cash flow windfall could prove much smaller than expected.

extraction.body: Hackers tied to the record Binance theft have begun converting a large slice of the stolen XRP into bitcoin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said in an update dated through Friday, with about 42 million XRP — roughly $50 million — already swapped, mostly through THORChain. Converted bitcoin from other stolen assets nearly doubled overnight to about 1,650 BTC, worth some $124 million, Elliptic wrote . Most of that jump came from the XRP route. About 192 million XRP, roughly $226 million, remained unswapped in addresses linked to the Binance theft. The XRP was part of the Oct. 29 drain that Binance later put at $6.34 billion. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC that day, five hot wallets sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker address. The FBI has attributed the campaign to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has reopened withdrawals in stages and said it has frozen or intercepted about $2.85 billion while covering customer losses from its own funds. The stolen XRP sat quiet at first. Early on Nov. 2, between 02:12 and 04:00 UTC, all about 233 million XRP moved into six new addresses, where it stayed until Nov. 5, Elliptic said . From the afternoon of Nov. 5, two of those six addresses began sending XRP on to dozens of new accounts that swapped it, mostly through THORChain into bitcoin. A small amount of ether also went through THORChain into bitcoin that evening. The main bitcoin and ether holdings from the theft — the largest pools — have still not moved, Elliptic said. That pattern matches what the firm saw after the Bybit hack: turn freezable and mid-liquidity tokens into bitcoin first, then attempt cash-out later through OTC brokers. The broader laundering trail is already vast. Since the Binance theft, Elliptic has counted more than 20,000 wallets on 16 blockchains, at least 36 services and at least 65,000 transactions — roughly one new wallet every 30 seconds and one transaction every 10 seconds. About $3.11 billion remains in addresses linked to the Binance theft, mostly as ether and bitcoin. A negligible amount has likely been cashed out so far. Issuers can freeze many stablecoins. They cannot freeze XRP the same way, and they cannot freeze bitcoin. After Tether and Circle locked down large stablecoin tranches on Oct. 29, the attacker prioritized assets that sit outside that kill switch. Swapping XRP into bitcoin continues that logic: bitcoin is harder to claw back once it is fragmented across fresh addresses. All of the stolen SOL, about $87 million at Elliptic’s prices, has already been swapped, bridged or mixed, with much of it ending as bitcoin. Most early Tron laundering — about $220 million in TRX — has also run, a flow Bitcoin Magazine noted when covering the quiet shutdown of the T3 Financial Crime Unit before the hack. Only small parts of the main ether and NEAR piles have moved. Some converted bitcoin has gone into Wasabi-style coinjoins — about 33 BTC, or $2.5 million, since Nov. 1 — and about $1.1 million in ether and SOL entered the Privacy Cash pool before that service paused deposits. Elliptic said the speed points to conventional automation, not an AI agent making live decisions: fixed timing, set amounts, blind retries and new tactics introduced hours apart. U.S. bank supervisors have already checked in with lenders after the Binance breach. For bitcoin markets, the nearer question is how much more of the remaining ~192 million XRP — and eventually the parked ether — gets turned into BTC before anyone tries to cash out. The test now is whether THORChain operators and other bridges keep blocking the published attacker addresses fast enough to slow the XRP-to-bitcoin pipe, or whether the rest of that pile follows the same overnight path the first $50 million already took. sources.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
passages: A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic.
According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September.
To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference.
Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.
In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna.

Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million.
Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.
“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch.

“That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”
Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion.
The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies.
OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things.
AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies.
“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns.
There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights.
As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”

extraction.body: Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it. A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month. As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed. “Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.” Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said. Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000. “If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.” “The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued. October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong. Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace. “OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets. Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market. Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition. “Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp. “For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.” The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty. “As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.” Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.” tokens go brrr costs go ahhh pic.twitter.com/1whCWCJCyM “A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.” Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion. Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one. Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend. Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI , SpaceXAI , and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct . Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth. “The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.” Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck in 2027 Sean O'Kane Claude can now analyze your spending with its new Personal Finance tool Aisha Malik Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows Aditya Mehta New York City’s Mamdani criticizes Madison Square Garden owner over surveillance tech Zack Whittaker Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI Julie Bort New York Times and other outlets sue web browser Brave over alleged content scraping Rebecca Bellan

To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference.
Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.
In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna.

Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million.

“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch.

“That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”
Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion.
The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies.
OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things.
AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies.
“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns.
There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights.
As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”

extraction.body: Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it. A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month. As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed. “Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.” Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said. Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000. “If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.” “The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued. October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong. Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace. “OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets. Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market. Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition. “Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp. “For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.” The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty. “As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.” Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.” Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one. Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. passages: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.
Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.
He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip.
Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.
“Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment.
But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational.
Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.
In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips.
They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that.
So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.
The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates.
It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens.
Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences.

extraction.body: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. sources.title: After blocking Muse, Amazon now lets users text Alexa to help them shop
passages: Amazon is jumping on the currently most popular bandwagon for interacting with AI agents: texting.
The e-commerce giant said select U.S. customers will get a text asking them to enable the shopping feature.
Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing.

The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa , and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders.
Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon.
The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September.
The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season.
The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly.
As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction.

Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September , further.

Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing.

The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa , and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders.
Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon.
The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September.
The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season.
The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly.
As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction.

Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September , further.

extraction.body: Amazon is jumping on the currently most popular bandwagon for interacting with AI agents: texting. The company on Friday said it is launching a feature that lets customers chat with its Alexa AI agent over text messages to help them shop, much like you can with AI agents like Muse or Instinct. The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September. The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season. The e-commerce giant said select U.S. customers will get a text asking them to enable the shopping feature. Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing. The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa , and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders. Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon. The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly. The company said users who don’t get invited to use this feature can sign up to a waitlist . The feature will be rolled out more broadly in the coming weeks. As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction. Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September , further.

sources.title: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
passages: The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end.
When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.
Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.

As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)
Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.
The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action.
His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)

extraction.body: Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday. First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user. While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character. The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it. As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.) The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!) When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them. Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device. sources.title: The Duo apps are coming, says Apple
passages: The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch.
But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front.

The Duo has also proven to be more popular than perhaps Apple had planned for, given its high price point. (It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.) The device quickly sold out within hours of orders opening up, and now, Duo ship times have shifted into the next year.
On its earnings call this week, Apple said it’s “hard to predict” when the Duo constraints leading to those delays will improve .
The company said that more than 2,000 app developers attended its over 50 in-person workshops that were hosted across 19 cities worldwide.

“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation,” said Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations, in a statement referring to the 100,000-app milestone. “The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo,” she added.
Spotify, for instance, is still showing the black bar on the side, and the App Store doesn’t yet say an update is available on our review unit of the Duo.
However, given that this list comes directly from Apple, we expect to see these updates soon.

sources.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
passages: The company said later that day that an investigation two days earlier (on Monday) had revealed that “certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor.” It also said it had detected “abnormal activity” and, in response, took down its login page and know-your-transaction service, which monitors threats to cryptocurrency holdings in real time.
The company has also removed access to its Reactor and Data Solutions services.
Also known as an adversary-in-the-middle attack, on-path attacks happen when a hacker gains access to a piece of infrastructure sending traffic back and forth between two parties.
Chainalysis has yet to say where the infrastructure compromise occurred and if the data obtained from it was TLS encrypted.
It asked customers to submit their trusted IP addresses so they can be added to an allow list and to prepare to reset credentials once they regain access.
The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools.

An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It’s not clear why the company considered such information “non-sensitive.”

Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays.
