sources.title: AI is the new dating dealbreaker

extraction.body: When Irene moved to San Francisco last year, she started using dating apps as a way to meet new people, get to know her new city, and connect with others who care about the things she does. “Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls. “Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’” Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design. Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.” In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another. Over the past month, I bopped around the city, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene. For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza. Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely. In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over. “A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” Kyle says, raising his gaze and looking off into the distance. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future,” he says. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he says. But Bryan, who works at a frontier AI company and also asked to go by a pseudonym, doesn’t believe that feelings about AI matter when it comes to romance. To him, dating is more about weighing a series of factors: how someone talks and approaches problems, how they have fun. But, he says, “The one way it interacts is that there are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.” Bryan isn’t exactly wrong about the benefits of a high-paying job in AI. With the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI in the next year, matchmakers have found that clients are specifying “AI engineer” on their list of preferred dating profile qualifications. And stability is particularly attractive right now: According to a CBRE report released in August, more than 20,000 AI jobs were added to the San Francisco Bay Area’s technology workforce, even as overall tech talent contracted by 6 percent since 2022. “Member of technical staff” roles have become very lucrative jobs; the average salary of an AI researcher can be around $300,000. According to the New York Post, one matchmaker found that her client booked a six-month stay in San Francisco because of the possibility of meeting a significant other who might be connected to an AI company going through an IPO. According to a study released by Elon University, 27 percent of Americans are turning to AI chatbots with personal, emotional, or social queries. Thirty-eight percent of the surveyed group said they occasionally tell AI things that they would not tell other people, including their romantic partners. Andromeda weighs the pros and cons of dating someone who would use bots for “emotional regulation.” “Socially and psychologically, it’s a big deal, and we have to talk about it,” she says. “I would certainly date a man who uses AI to talk through intense thoughts and feelings and to brainstorm clarity.” At the same time, she is also reluctant to date someone who might abuse a chatbot, since it’s maladaptive behavior and does not represent good values for model welfare. “If they treat ChatGPT badly today, it will be me tomorrow!” If Andromeda worries about what people tell chatbots, others have gone a step further and let AI do the talking for them. At the Hugging Face Open Source Week party, Joseph, a 21-year-old software engineer, explains how he has automated his dating life. Working 14 hours a day to launch his startup, he has decided to outsource swiping on Hinge entirely to an AI agent. The agent is managed by his human virtual assistant from the Philippines and has been fine-tuned to mimic the way that he speaks and acts. Looking at each profile, the AI agent sends tailored outreach messages to spark a conversation. After some back and forth, the agent determines if the woman is compatible with Joseph and, if so, books open slots on his weekend calendars for dating in person. “It’s kind of a copy-and-paste sequence that happens with every girl to get to know about you, understand your backstory, and so on and so forth.” He’s not alone. A 2025 survey by Match and the Kinsey Institute found that 26 percent of singles in the United States use AI tools to enhance their dating experiences. Hinge now has an AI tool to generate suggested responses and Bumble, which will soon phase out swiping, has launched Bee, an AI assistant-facilitated matchmaking tool. (Bumble VP of Communications Natalie Logan said in an email that Bumble has not yet announced the update to the swipe, and that Bee operates independently of that update.) “It has been extremely successful. The overall process has lowered what he calls “CPN,” or “cost per nut.” At 29 years old, JJ has stopped using dating apps. Instead, she turns to the Date-Me Directory — a collection of longform, resume-like documents where people write personal dating profiles — to find a partner. Two years ago, she worked in product design in New York, but she transitioned into the AI safety field because she felt that it aligned more with her effective altruist morals. “Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls.
“Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’” Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design.

Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.” In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT.
Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another.

Over the past month, I bopped around the city, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene.

For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza.

Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely.
In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over.
“A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” Kyle says, raising his gaze and looking off into the distance.
“For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future,” he says.
“They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he says.
But Bryan, who works at a frontier AI company and also asked to go by a pseudonym, doesn’t believe that feelings about AI matter when it comes to romance.
To him, dating is more about weighing a series of factors: how someone talks and approaches problems, how they have fun.

But, he says, “The one way it interacts is that there are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.” Bryan isn’t exactly wrong about the benefits of a high-paying job in AI.
With the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI in the next year, matchmakers have found that clients are specifying “AI engineer” on their list of preferred dating profile qualifications.

And stability is particularly attractive right now: According to a CBRE report released in August, more than 20,000 AI jobs were added to the San Francisco Bay Area’s technology workforce, even as overall tech talent contracted by 6 percent since 2022.
“Member of technical staff” roles have become very lucrative jobs; the average salary of an AI researcher can be around $300,000.

According to the New York Post, one matchmaker found that her client booked a six-month stay in San Francisco because of the possibility of meeting a significant other who might be connected to an AI company going through an IPO.
According to a study released by Elon University, 27 percent of Americans are turning to AI chatbots with personal, emotional, or social queries.
Thirty-eight percent of the surveyed group said they occasionally tell AI things that they would not tell other people, including their romantic partners.
Andromeda weighs the pros and cons of dating someone who would use bots for “emotional regulation.” “Socially and psychologically, it’s a big deal, and we have to talk about it,” she says.

“I would certainly date a man who uses AI to talk through intense thoughts and feelings and to brainstorm clarity.” At the same time, she is also reluctant to date someone who might abuse a chatbot, since it’s maladaptive behavior and does not represent good values for model welfare.
“If they treat ChatGPT badly today, it will be me tomorrow!” If Andromeda worries about what people tell chatbots, others have gone a step further and let AI do the talking for them.

After some back and forth, the agent determines if the woman is compatible with Joseph and, if so, books open slots on his weekend calendars for dating in person.
“It’s kind of a copy-and-paste sequence that happens with every girl to get to know about you, understand your backstory, and so on and so forth.” He’s not alone.

Hinge now has an AI tool to generate suggested responses and Bumble, which will soon phase out swiping, has launched Bee, an AI assistant-facilitated matchmaking tool. (Bumble VP of Communications Natalie Logan said in an email that Bumble has not yet announced the update to the swipe, and that Bee operates independently of that update.) “It has been extremely successful.
The overall process has lowered what he calls “CPN,” or “cost per nut.” At 29 years old, JJ has stopped using dating apps.
Instead, she turns to the Date-Me Directory — a collection of longform, resume-like documents where people write personal dating profiles — to find a partner.
Two years ago, she worked in product design in New York, but she transitioned into the AI safety field because she felt that it aligned more with her effective altruist morals.

passages: Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.
The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them.
The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July.

extraction.body: Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets. The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.” In a blog post , cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in. Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet. The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network. Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September . Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies. Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October , which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.” Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication. The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets. Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

extraction.body: Democrats’ historic victories in this week’s U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry. The public voted on 41 data center-related ballot measures on Tuesday — in all but one, the majority voted to impose more restrictions on data center development. And even when data centers weren’t on the ballot directly, they were a major talking point, with newly-elected Democratic governors and congressmembers likely to support additional regulation . On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and Anthony Ha discuss what the election will mean for the tech industry moving forward — not just when it comes to data centers (which OpenAI is already trying to rebrand ), but also increased government scrutiny of Big Tech.

extraction.body: AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer. One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large. The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models. You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music. All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download. While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts. This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark , a 167MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation. Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog , told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data. “I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto . In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.

passages: His new venture, Physicl , has raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations.

Physicl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits.
There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.
In particular, Physicl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases.
The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects.
It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems.
For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.
SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week.

SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers.
Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult.

“The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state.

extraction.body: Alex de Vigan’s last business got swamped by the rise of generative AI, but now he’s betting the tech that team had built, a platform for creating tempting product renderings for e-commerce, can be re-purposed to make robots more useful. His new venture, Physicl , has raised $10 million in seed funding led by Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations. Founder and CEO de Vigan spent the last decade building nfinite, which made it easy for brands and retailers to create 3D models of their goods and display them online. The arrival of transformer-based AI models led that company to focus more on generative imagery, but de Vigan saw a new purpose for his team and the tech stack they’d built to faithfully render 3D environments. “What we were super unique about doing in 3D, AI was going to replace, but something was missing in AI: its ability to understand, interact, and manipulate space and objects,” de Vigan says. Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations. Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. De Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective. Physicl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise. In particular, Physicl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow. SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers. However, Physicl wants to be more than a data provider; it sees itself as the tooling for ongoing synthetic data generation. “What we created 10 years ago, without knowing it, was basically an agentic workflow to transform unstructured information into high-fidelity 3D,” de Vigan said. He imagines customers bringing trillions of images or millions of hours of lidar capture data to feed into his platform and turn them into high-quality 3D representations that can be used to generate billions of permutations to train their models. “The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state. That, to me, is super exciting, and this is exactly what Physicl is offering.”

Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations.

Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. De Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective.

Physicl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.

In particular, Physicl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.

SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers.

However, Physicl wants to be more than a data provider; it sees itself as the tooling for ongoing synthetic data generation. “What we created 10 years ago, without knowing it, was basically an agentic workflow to transform unstructured information into high-fidelity 3D,” de Vigan said. He imagines customers bringing trillions of images or millions of hours of lidar capture data to feed into his platform and turn them into high-quality 3D representations that can be used to generate billions of permutations to train their models.

“The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state. That, to me, is super exciting, and this is exactly what Physicl is offering.”

passages: OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported.
OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.

The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential.
That valuation does not include new capital raised.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering.
In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation.
OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering .
Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person.
Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO.

That valuation does not include new capital raised. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said. Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public." Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported. The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation. The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.

OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.

Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.
The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut.

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public."

Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation.

That valuation does not include new capital raised.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering.

OpenAI just secured a massive bag, but it’s not what it expected. In a new funding round, OpenAI raises $11 billion to hit a valuation of $1.25 trillion. While it’s a jaw-dropping number, the deal values the ChatGPT maker lower than what the company was chasing only weeks ago.
The money landed on Friday, according to people familiar with the matter, as first reported here. And more could follow soon. So why does a trillion-dollar raise feel like a step back?

The $11 billion is only the opening tranche. The full round could reach about $20 billion, with the rest expected to close over the coming weeks. However, in late September, OpenAI was reportedly targeting $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation.

Both figures have since been dropped as the AI market faces some setbacks. As a result, roughly $10 billion in new capital and $150 billion have been shaved off OpenAI’s valuation. Still, the company remains up there, raising $122 billion at an $852 billion valuation in March this year.

Even after the cut, its value has jumped nearly 47% in about eight months. Few companies on earth can say that. Put simply, OpenAI is still growing fast. It’s just growing slower than its own ambitions.

The first tranche was reportedly led by Coatue Management and T. Rowe Price. SoftBank Group, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund, Andreessen Horowitz and a UAE investor group also joined in.
You’ll recognize most of those names. Many have backed OpenAI before. Their return tells you big money still believes in the long game, even at a lower price.

There’s another twist worth watching. OpenAI is said to be working with investment banks to open the round to high-net-worth and retail investors. If that happens, regular investors could grab a slice of a company that’s usually off-limits until it lists.
It comes down to market sentiment. AI stocks have taken a beating on public markets. Investors are asking tougher questions about whether massive infrastructure spending will actually pay off.
And since the US midterm elections, worries have grown about new hurdles for data center construction. Regulation is now on a lot of minds. OpenAI isn’t alone, either.

Rival Anthropic is reportedly feeling similar pressure, with potential IPO buyers eyeing a valuation well below its hopes. When two of AI’s biggest names both reset expectations, it says a lot about the wider market.

Private valuations like these often hint at where public markets are heading. A trimmed target suggests investors now want proof, not just promises. Also, OpenAI pushed back its plans to go public, and a listing is now widely expected sometime in 2027.

This cash buys it time. Third, it’s a reality check for the whole AI trade. If you hold tech stocks, AI-themed funds, or even crypto tokens riding the AI narrative, sentiment around OpenAI ripples straight into your portfolio.

The bottom line? OpenAI can still raise money at a scale almost nobody else can match. But the era of valuations that only go up may be taking a breather. Watch how the remaining $9 billion lands. It could set the tone for AI investing heading into 2027.

coreStoryFacts.text: (Bloomberg) -- OpenAI has closed on new funding of roughly $11 billion, the initial part of a round that values the company at $1.25 trillion, according to people familiar with the matter.The funding was wired to the company as of Friday, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public.

The remainder of the round, which could increase to as much as $20 billion in total, is expected to be completed in the coming weeks, one person said.The AI developer has been in talks for more than a month to raise a large funding round after delaying its plans for an initial public offering.
The Wall Street Journal previously reported some details of the funding.
The reduced funding goals represent a stark shift for a fundraising juggernaut that helped usher in the current AI boom.
OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted.
Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
The current figures fall well short of that target.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans.
There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.
It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round.
The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion.
That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization.
The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds.
That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others.
Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering.
However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal.
According to the Wall Street Journal , one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion.
Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter.
The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double.
The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday.

The money landed on Friday, according to people familiar with the matter, as first reported here. And more could follow soon. So why does a trillion-dollar raise feel like a step back?

The $11 billion is only the opening tranche. The full round could reach about $20 billion, with the rest expected to close over the coming weeks. However, in late September, OpenAI was reportedly targeting $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation.

Both figures have since been dropped as the AI market faces some setbacks. As a result, roughly $10 billion in new capital and $150 billion have been shaved off OpenAI’s valuation. Still, the company remains up there, raising $122 billion at an $852 billion valuation in March this year.

The first tranche was reportedly led by Coatue Management and T. Rowe Price. SoftBank Group, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund, Andreessen Horowitz and a UAE investor group also joined in.

And since the US midterm elections, worries have grown about new hurdles for data center construction. Regulation is now on a lot of minds. OpenAI isn’t alone, either.

Rival Anthropic is reportedly feeling similar pressure, with potential IPO buyers eyeing a valuation well below its hopes. When two of AI’s biggest names both reset expectations, it says a lot about the wider market.

facts.text: (Bloomberg) -- OpenAI has closed on new funding of roughly $11 billion, the initial part of a round that values the company at $1.25 trillion, according to people familiar with the matter.The funding was wired to the company as of Friday, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public.

The remainder of the round, which could increase to as much as $20 billion in total, is expected to be completed in the coming weeks, one person said.The AI developer has been in talks for more than a month to raise a large funding round after delaying its plans for an initial public offering.
The Wall Street Journal previously reported some details of the funding.
The reduced funding goals represent a stark shift for a fundraising juggernaut that helped usher in the current AI boom.
OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted.
Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
The current figures fall well short of that target.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans.
There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.
It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round.
The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion.
That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization.
The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds.
That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others.
Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering.
However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal.
According to the Wall Street Journal , one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion.
Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter.
The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double.
The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday.
OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox.
Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra.
Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well.
The company plans to go public sometime in 2027.
Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the listing.
In July, The Information reported that the ChatGPT developer has more than $665 billion worth of chip and data center commitments.
OpenAI just secured a massive bag, but it’s not what it expected.
In a new funding round, OpenAI raises $11 billion to hit a valuation of $1.25 trillion.
While it’s a jaw-dropping number, the deal values the ChatGPT maker lower than what the company was chasing only weeks ago.
The full round could reach about $20 billion, with the rest expected to close over the coming weeks.
However, in late September, OpenAI was reportedly targeting $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation.
OpenAI can still raise money at a scale almost nobody else can match.
As a result, roughly $10 billion in new capital and $150 billion have been shaved off OpenAI’s valuation.
Still, the company remains up there, raising $122 billion at an $852 billion valuation in March this year.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks Inc. (PANW) is negotiating to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli company that secures the digital credentials used by artificial intelligence agents, for roughly $500 million, according to people cited by The Information. The discussions are preliminary, and there is no assurance an agreement will be reached. If completed, the transaction would be the fifth acquisition the Santa Clara, California-based cybersecurity vendor has announced in 2026, as CEO Nikesh Arora pushes deeper into identity security and defenses built around autonomous AI systems. Clutch was founded in late 2023 by CEO Ofir Har-Chen, CTO Sagi Haas and R&D vice president Tal Kimhi. Its software tracks so-called non-human identities: the API keys, service accounts, tokens and passwords that let applications and automated tools talk to one another and reach corporate systems. As companies deploy AI agents that can read internal data and act on their own, the number of such credentials has multiplied, creating a new problem for security teams that must determine which agents have access, what they are allowed to do and whether their keys are being abused. The platform maps those identities across an organization's environment, flags excessive or exposed permissions, manages credentials through their lifecycle and detects suspicious use. Clutch has been extending the product to cover AI agents specifically. A purchase would build on Palo Alto's $25 billion takeover of CyberArk, completed in February 2026. CyberArk's business centers on controlling access for human employees, while Clutch addresses machine and agent credentials, making the two largely complementary rather than overlapping. Clutch has raised about $28.5 million in two disclosed rounds. Lightspeed Venture Partners led an $8.5 million seed round in July 2024, joined by Merlin Ventures and individual investors including Shlomo Kramer, Exabeam co-founder Nir Polak and HashiCorp co-founder Armon Dadgar. SignalFire led a $20 million Series A in January 2025, with Lightspeed and Merlin Ventures participating again. The company operates in Israel and the United States. At the reported price, a sale would be a sizable return for backers relative to capital raised, though Clutch's current valuation could not be determined and final terms remain unsettled. Palo Alto told The Information it does not discuss rumors or speculation. Clutch did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Palo Alto is scheduled to report results on Nov. 18. Analysts expect earnings of 97 cents a share, up from 93 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $3.31 billion versus $2.47 billion, according to consensus estimates cited in the coverage. The stock carries a consensus Buy rating and an average analyst price target of $414.17. Citigroup lifted its target to $440, and Wells Fargo raised its forecast to $525 in October. Shares trade at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 870, a premium that leaves little room for disappointment on growth. Note: Earnings and revenue figures are analyst consensus estimates ahead of the Nov. 18 report. The shares are widely held through cybersecurity and software funds. Palo Alto accounts for 9.02% of the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), 7.56% of the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) and 5.42% of the Amplify Cybersecurity ETF (HACK), so any re-rating tied to the deal or the earnings report would ripple through those products. For investors, the central question is whether Arora can keep paying up for tuck-in technology without straining a multiple already stretched by the CyberArk integration. Identity security has become one of the fastest-growing corners of the market as enterprises shift toward automated operations, and rivals including Microsoft and CrowdStrike are competing for the same budgets. A Clutch deal would be small relative to CyberArk, but it would signal that Palo Alto intends to own the agent-credential layer before larger competitors establish a foothold. If completed, the transaction would be the fifth acquisition the Santa Clara, California-based cybersecurity vendor has announced in 2026, as CEO Nikesh Arora pushes deeper into identity security and defenses built around autonomous AI systems.

Clutch was founded in late 2023 by CEO Ofir Har-Chen, CTO Sagi Haas and R&D vice president Tal Kimhi. Its software tracks so-called non-human identities: the API keys, service accounts, tokens and passwords that let applications and automated tools talk to one another and reach corporate systems. As companies deploy AI agents that can read internal data and act on their own, the number of such credentials has multiplied, creating a new problem for security teams that must determine which agents have access, what they are allowed to do and whether their keys are being abused.

The platform maps those identities across an organization's environment, flags excessive or exposed permissions, manages credentials through their lifecycle and detects suspicious use. Clutch has been extending the product to cover AI agents specifically.

A purchase would build on Palo Alto's $25 billion takeover of CyberArk, completed in February 2026. CyberArk's business centers on controlling access for human employees, while Clutch addresses machine and agent credentials, making the two largely complementary rather than overlapping.

Clutch has raised about $28.5 million in two disclosed rounds. Lightspeed Venture Partners led an $8.5 million seed round in July 2024, joined by Merlin Ventures and individual investors including Shlomo Kramer, Exabeam co-founder Nir Polak and HashiCorp co-founder Armon Dadgar. SignalFire led a $20 million Series A in January 2025, with Lightspeed and Merlin Ventures participating again. The company operates in Israel and the United States.

At the reported price, a sale would be a sizable return for backers relative to capital raised, though Clutch's current valuation could not be determined and final terms remain unsettled. Palo Alto told The Information it does not discuss rumors or speculation. Clutch did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Palo Alto is scheduled to report results on Nov. 18. Analysts expect earnings of 97 cents a share, up from 93 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $3.31 billion versus $2.47 billion, according to consensus estimates cited in the coverage.

The stock carries a consensus Buy rating and an average analyst price target of $414.17. Citigroup lifted its target to $440, and Wells Fargo raised its forecast to $525 in October. Shares trade at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 870, a premium that leaves little room for disappointment on growth.
Note: Earnings and revenue figures are analyst consensus estimates ahead of the Nov. 18 report.

The shares are widely held through cybersecurity and software funds. Palo Alto accounts for 9.02% of the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), 7.56% of the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) and 5.42% of the Amplify Cybersecurity ETF (HACK), so any re-rating tied to the deal or the earnings report would ripple through those products.

For investors, the central question is whether Arora can keep paying up for tuck-in technology without straining a multiple already stretched by the CyberArk integration. Identity security has become one of the fastest-growing corners of the market as enterprises shift toward automated operations, and rivals including Microsoft and CrowdStrike are competing for the same budgets. A Clutch deal would be small relative to CyberArk, but it would signal that Palo Alto intends to own the agent-credential layer before larger competitors establish a foothold.

passages: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market.

With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations.

Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security.
If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks.

The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions.
The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities.
As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore.
Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter. The deal would value the young company at nearly six times its last funding round valuation of $85 million and marks the latest mega-acquisition in the exploding AI security market. If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks. Palo Alto Networks is closing in on a roughly $500 million deal to buy Clutch, a startup focused on securing AI agents, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiations. The talks come as enterprise security vendors scramble to address the security risks posed by autonomous AI systems now being deployed across corporate environments. Clutch was last valued at just $85 million, meaning Palo Alto is willing to pay nearly six times that figure to acquire the technology. The startup, backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire, has built a platform specifically designed to monitor and secure AI agents - the autonomous software systems that can take actions, access data, and make decisions without human oversight. As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore. The deal talks reveal how quickly AI agent security has transformed from a niche concern into a must-have capability for enterprise security platforms. Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market. Palo Alto Networks has been methodically building its AI security portfolio through a combination of internal development and strategic acquisitions. The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions. The valuation jump reflects both Clutch's technology and the broader market dynamics. Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security. Even Nvidia has entered the space, launching an open agent safety platform that provides full-stack governance for AI systems. For Palo Alto Networks, the acquisition would address a critical gap in its product lineup at a moment when customers are demanding comprehensive AI security solutions. The company competes directly with CrowdStrike, Fortinet, and other security vendors who are all racing to offer end-to-end protection for AI deployments. Losing ground in this emerging category could mean losing access to the next generation of enterprise security budgets. Lightspeed and SignalFire, Clutch's primary backers, stand to see substantial returns if the deal closes at the reported $500 million figure. Both firms have been active investors in the AI security space, betting early that protecting autonomous systems would become a major enterprise priority. The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities. The deal structure and timeline remain fluid, and there's no guarantee the talks will result in a completed transaction. But the momentum is clear: enterprise security is being rebuilt around AI, and the companies that can't secure autonomous agents risk becoming irrelevant. Palo Alto Networks appears determined not to let that happen, even if it means paying a significant premium for a startup that was valued at a fraction of the purchase price just months ago. Early AI security concerns focused on model vulnerabilities, data poisoning, and prompt injection attacks. But as companies move from chatbots to autonomous agents that can access systems, move data, and take actions on behalf of users, the security model has to evolve. Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces. Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Clutch at a 6x valuation premium signals that AI agent security has moved from emerging concern to existential priority for enterprise security vendors. With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations. As AI agents proliferate across corporate networks, expect more acquisitions, more funding rounds, and more competition for the startups building the guardrails that make autonomous AI safe for enterprise deployment.

The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.

Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

(PANW) is negotiating to buy Clutch Security, an Israeli company that secures the digital credentials used by artificial intelligence agents, for roughly $500 million, according to people cited by The Information. The discussions are preliminary, and there is no assurance an agreement will be reached. If completed, the transaction would be the fifth acquisition the Santa Clara, California-based cybersecurity vendor has announced in 2026, as CEO Nikesh Arora pushes deeper into identity security and defenses built around autonomous AI systems. Clutch was founded in late 2023 by CEO Ofir Har-Chen, CTO Sagi Haas and R&D vice president Tal Kimhi. Its software tracks so-called non-human identities: the API keys, service accounts, tokens and passwords that let applications and automated tools talk to one another and reach corporate systems. As companies deploy AI agents that can read internal data and act on their own, the number of such credentials has multiplied, creating a new problem for security teams that must determine which agents have access, what they are allowed to do and whether their keys are being abused. The platform maps those identities across an organization's environment, flags excessive or exposed permissions, manages credentials through their lifecycle and detects suspicious use. Clutch has been extending the product to cover AI agents specifically. A purchase would build on Palo Alto's $25 billion takeover of CyberArk, completed in February 2026. CyberArk's business centers on controlling access for human employees, while Clutch addresses machine and agent credentials, making the two largely complementary rather than overlapping. Clutch has raised about $28.5 million in two disclosed rounds. Lightspeed Venture Partners led an $8.5 million seed round in July 2024, joined by Merlin Ventures and individual investors including Shlomo Kramer, Exabeam co-founder Nir Polak and HashiCorp co-founder Armon Dadgar. SignalFire led a $20 million Series A in January 2025, with Lightspeed and Merlin Ventures participating again. The company operates in Israel and the United States. At the reported price, a sale would be a sizable return for backers relative to capital raised, though Clutch's current valuation could not be determined and final terms remain unsettled. Palo Alto told The Information it does not discuss rumors or speculation. Clutch did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Palo Alto is scheduled to report results on Nov. 18. Analysts expect earnings of 97 cents a share, up from 93 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $3.31 billion versus $2.47 billion, according to consensus estimates cited in the coverage. The stock carries a consensus Buy rating and an average analyst price target of $414.17. Citigroup lifted its target to $440, and Wells Fargo raised its forecast to $525 in October. Shares trade at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of about 870, a premium that leaves little room for disappointment on growth. Note: Earnings and revenue figures are analyst consensus estimates ahead of the Nov. 18 report. The shares are widely held through cybersecurity and software funds. Palo Alto accounts for 9.02% of the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), 7.56% of the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) and 5.42% of the Amplify Cybersecurity ETF (HACK), so any re-rating tied to the deal or the earnings report would ripple through those products. For investors, the central question is whether Arora can keep paying up for tuck-in technology without straining a multiple already stretched by the CyberArk integration. Identity security has become one of the fastest-growing corners of the market as enterprises shift toward automated operations, and rivals including Microsoft and CrowdStrike are competing for the same budgets. A Clutch deal would be small relative to CyberArk, but it would signal that Palo Alto intends to own the agent-credential layer before larger competitors establish a foothold. passages: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market.

With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations.

Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security.
If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks.

The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions.
The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities.
As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore.
Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces.

extraction.body: Palo Alto Networks is in advanced talks to acquire Clutch, an AI agent security startup, for roughly $500 million, according to sources familiar with the matter. The deal would value the young company at nearly six times its last funding round valuation of $85 million and marks the latest mega-acquisition in the exploding AI security market. If completed, the purchase would give the enterprise security giant a critical foothold in protecting the autonomous AI agents now flooding corporate networks. Palo Alto Networks is closing in on a roughly $500 million deal to buy Clutch, a startup focused on securing AI agents, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiations. The talks come as enterprise security vendors scramble to address the security risks posed by autonomous AI systems now being deployed across corporate environments. Clutch was last valued at just $85 million, meaning Palo Alto is willing to pay nearly six times that figure to acquire the technology. The startup, backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners and SignalFire, has built a platform specifically designed to monitor and secure AI agents - the autonomous software systems that can take actions, access data, and make decisions without human oversight. As companies rush to deploy these agents for everything from customer service to code generation, the security implications have become impossible to ignore. The deal talks reveal how quickly AI agent security has transformed from a niche concern into a must-have capability for enterprise security platforms. Just days ago, CrowdStrike dropped $500M on AI security duo Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in a double acquisition targeting the exact same market. Palo Alto Networks has been methodically building its AI security portfolio through a combination of internal development and strategic acquisitions. The company's existing platform already includes some AI-focused security tools, but Clutch would bring specialized capabilities for monitoring AI agent behavior, detecting anomalies, and preventing autonomous systems from accessing sensitive data or taking unauthorized actions. The valuation jump reflects both Clutch's technology and the broader market dynamics. Venture investors have poured billions into AI security startups over the past year, with companies like Armadin - founded by former FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia - raising $255.5M at a $2.5B valuation to build AI agent swarms for enterprise security. Even Nvidia has entered the space, launching an open agent safety platform that provides full-stack governance for AI systems. For Palo Alto Networks, the acquisition would address a critical gap in its product lineup at a moment when customers are demanding comprehensive AI security solutions. The company competes directly with CrowdStrike, Fortinet, and other security vendors who are all racing to offer end-to-end protection for AI deployments. Losing ground in this emerging category could mean losing access to the next generation of enterprise security budgets. Lightspeed and SignalFire, Clutch's primary backers, stand to see substantial returns if the deal closes at the reported $500 million figure. Both firms have been active investors in the AI security space, betting early that protecting autonomous systems would become a major enterprise priority. The rapid exit timeline - Clutch is still a relatively young company - suggests just how urgent the need has become for established security vendors to acquire rather than build these capabilities. The deal structure and timeline remain fluid, and there's no guarantee the talks will result in a completed transaction. But the momentum is clear: enterprise security is being rebuilt around AI, and the companies that can't secure autonomous agents risk becoming irrelevant. Palo Alto Networks appears determined not to let that happen, even if it means paying a significant premium for a startup that was valued at a fraction of the purchase price just months ago. Early AI security concerns focused on model vulnerabilities, data poisoning, and prompt injection attacks. But as companies move from chatbots to autonomous agents that can access systems, move data, and take actions on behalf of users, the security model has to evolve. Clutch's technology addresses this next phase, providing the guardrails enterprises need to deploy AI agents without creating massive new attack surfaces. Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Clutch at a 6x valuation premium signals that AI agent security has moved from emerging concern to existential priority for enterprise security vendors. With CrowdStrike, Nvidia, and now Palo Alto all making aggressive moves in this space within weeks of each other, the message to enterprises is clear: autonomous AI systems require fundamentally new security approaches, and the companies that provide them will command premium valuations. As AI agents proliferate across corporate networks, expect more acquisitions, more funding rounds, and more competition for the startups building the guardrails that make autonomous AI safe for enterprise deployment.

facts.text: Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security , a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired.
Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million , Calcalist reported.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source.
The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.

sources.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
passages: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers.
Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent.
Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab.
Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it.
I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents.
Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week.
On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months.
During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot , which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

The Tamagotchi-like gadget is designed for people who don't wear Meta's smart glasses, and Zuckerberg called it the fastest way to talk to Muse without wearing them. SEE ALSO: Meet the Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3, starting at $249 The reveal was set up earlier in the keynote. During a live demo, Zuckerberg used Meta's glasses to talk with his customized Muse assistant, which he'd named Agrippa, about a handheld device he was working on. That device turned out to be Muse Charm.Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Zuckerberg also suggested Meta could eventually collect a small fee on transactions the assistant helps complete.Muse Charm will ship by the holidays in December, according to Zuckerberg. Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later.The device enters a category with a rocky track record. Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year. Muse Charm's main selling point is that it runs on the same assistant as Meta's glasses.
