extraction.body: Meta announced on November 6, 2026 that spaces are now available everywhere Muse is available, letting users create persistent, customized experiences inside the app by describing an idea and refining the result with Muse. Each space becomes a saved part of the app that can support routines, goals, interests, practical work, or entertainment. Meta’s introductory examples include a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, and a planning board for a do-it-yourself project, illustrating the range between organizational tools and lightweight interactive experiences. Creation begins with a description supplied to Muse . The initial result serves as a starting point: users can continue working with Muse to add missing elements, try a different appearance, or change how the space functions. This allows the experience to evolve as its purpose becomes clearer, while preserving it as something the user can revisit. Users also control how spaces fit into the broader interface. They can place them in the sidebar or main tabs, hide those they do not currently need, and schedule when particular spaces appear. One scheduling example keeps a weekly planner prominent during the workweek and then replaces it with weekend plans. The controls therefore cover both the contents of a space and its prominence within the app. The suggested uses extend across personal organization, entertainment, and business activity. A shopping hub can combine holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists drawn from Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, and buyer messages in one view. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually. Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices. Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services. Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives. Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals. Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation. Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine. Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models. Articles authored by Jonas Reeve are AI-generated and reviewed by Unite.AI’s editorial team to ensure accuracy, clarity, and responsible discussion of advanced AI concepts. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually.

Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices.

Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services.

Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives.

Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals.

Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation.

Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine.

Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI , focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers.
Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent.
Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab.
Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it.
I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents.
Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week.
On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months.
During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
Meta has added Spaces to Muse, its AI agent, allowing users to describe ideas in chat and have the agent build trackers, planners, or project boards.
Spaces can connect to third-party apps to stay automatically updated without manual intervention.
According to TechCrunch , Spaces are topic-focused conversations that sit in the sidebar of the Muse interface, where the agent works toward a specific goal for the user.
Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg posted on X that he had been using Spaces and had built a BBQ game, an event tracker and a home control dashboard.
"Tell Muse what you need and it builds it," he wrote.
Spaces arrives a day after Meta introduced Muse Voice, which lets users video chat with their agent and give it spoken commands.
TechCrunch reports that on Meta's October earnings call, Zuckerberg said Muse agents had reached 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada less than two months after launch.
TechCrunch names OpenAI's dots and SpaceXAI's Grokbot as competing agent products.
Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask. — Meta

That device turned out to be Muse Charm.Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year. Muse Charm's main selling point is that it runs on the same assistant as Meta's glasses.

extraction.body: Meta announced on November 6, 2026 that spaces are now available everywhere Muse is available, letting users create persistent, customized experiences inside the app by describing an idea and refining the result with Muse. Each space becomes a saved part of the app that can support routines, goals, interests, practical work, or entertainment. Meta’s introductory examples include a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, and a planning board for a do-it-yourself project, illustrating the range between organizational tools and lightweight interactive experiences. Creation begins with a description supplied to Muse . The initial result serves as a starting point: users can continue working with Muse to add missing elements, try a different appearance, or change how the space functions. This allows the experience to evolve as its purpose becomes clearer, while preserving it as something the user can revisit. Users also control how spaces fit into the broader interface. They can place them in the sidebar or main tabs, hide those they do not currently need, and schedule when particular spaces appear. One scheduling example keeps a weekly planner prominent during the workweek and then replaces it with weekend plans. The controls therefore cover both the contents of a space and its prominence within the app. The suggested uses extend across personal organization, entertainment, and business activity. A shopping hub can combine holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists drawn from Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, and buyer messages in one view. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually. Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices. Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services. Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives. Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals. Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation. Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind. passages: Meta announced on November 6, 2026 that spaces are now available everywhere Muse is available, letting users create persistent, customized experiences inside the app by describing an idea and refining the result with Muse.

Each space becomes a saved part of the app that can support routines, goals, interests, practical work, or entertainment. Meta’s introductory examples include a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, and a planning board for a do-it-yourself project, illustrating the range between organizational tools and lightweight interactive experiences.

Creation begins with a description supplied to Muse . The initial result serves as a starting point: users can continue working with Muse to add missing elements, try a different appearance, or change how the space functions. This allows the experience to evolve as its purpose becomes clearer, while preserving it as something the user can revisit.

Users also control how spaces fit into the broader interface. They can place them in the sidebar or main tabs, hide those they do not currently need, and schedule when particular spaces appear. One scheduling example keeps a weekly planner prominent during the workweek and then replaces it with weekend plans. The controls therefore cover both the contents of a space and its prominence within the app.

The suggested uses extend across personal organization, entertainment, and business activity. A shopping hub can combine holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists drawn from Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, and buyer messages in one view. A school dashboard can find relevant events in school emails and add them to a calendar, reducing the need to assemble that schedule manually.

Other examples include a music tracker for releases and upcoming shows, a wedding planner containing RSVPs and vendor invoices, and a trip planner for reservations and daily itineraries. For business users, Meta suggests an order tracker that brings together new orders, customer messages, and items needing shipment, as well as a freelance client hub for projects, deadlines, and invoices.

Connecting apps allows spaces to update in the background. New concert dates, price changes, and savings progress can appear without the user requesting each update. People can also check off items, add notes, and make edits directly inside a space, with that work remaining when they return. The saved experience consequently combines conversational creation, direct interaction, and changing information from connected services.

Alongside spaces, Meta AI Research introduced specialized versions of the company’s existing models, trained using Muse Wonder , for people using Muse and Meta AI. Meta says the models incorporate Active Memory, which is intended to retain relevant earlier information and distinguish temporary, permanent, current, and stale information. Active Focus is intended to keep work moving toward a goal when unexpected obstacles arise by trying harder, recovering, or finding alternatives.

Meta reports that the current Muse model scores 47% on its Personal Superintelligence Index, compared with 38% for the previous model. On its Active Memory evaluation, Meta reports that the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% previously. The company also reports a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information needed to help users achieve their goals.

Meta additionally reports a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks when unexpected issues arise. The specialized models are designed to handle multitasking, decide when to pursue goals independently or collaborate live, and adapt to steering and clarifications during running tasks. In Meta AI , the corresponding changes are intended to break complex problems into steps, produce sharper follow-up questions, and accommodate changes of direction during a conversation.

Sharing and collaborative spaces remain under exploration, leaving the immediate release centered on individual customization. The broader product change is the combination of a reusable interface, connected information that stays current, and models intended to retain context and pursue goals. That makes continuity across visits, rather than the initial act of creation alone, central to whether spaces become durable parts of a user’s routine.

story.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent

facts.text: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers.
Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent.
Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab.
Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it.
I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents.
Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week.
On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months.
During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
Meta has added Spaces to Muse, its AI agent, allowing users to describe ideas in chat and have the agent build trackers, planners, or project boards.
Spaces can connect to third-party apps to stay automatically updated without manual intervention.
According to TechCrunch , Spaces are topic-focused conversations that sit in the sidebar of the Muse interface, where the agent works toward a specific goal for the user.
Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg posted on X that he had been using Spaces and had built a BBQ game, an event tracker and a home control dashboard.
"Tell Muse what you need and it builds it," he wrote.
Spaces arrives a day after Meta introduced Muse Voice, which lets users video chat with their agent and give it spoken commands.
TechCrunch reports that on Meta's October earnings call, Zuckerberg said Muse agents had reached 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada less than two months after launch.
TechCrunch names OpenAI's dots and SpaceXAI's Grokbot as competing agent products.
Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask. — Meta

passages: Nothing is preparing to launch its first AI-native device in December, and CEO Carl Pei says it will have no screen.
Pei has offered few details about the upcoming product, but describes it as a standalone tool rather than another AI-powered app.

Pei announced the launch in a post on X, describing the device as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.” He added that it “has no screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Nothing has not disclosed the product’s form, features, price, or exact launch date.
The only concrete detail is the absence of a display, alongside a teaser image showing the Nothing logo and an ambiguous black rounded corner.
The announcement comes a little over a year after Pei first outlined Nothing’s plans for AI-native devices and an AI operating system.
There have been rumors that Nothing is developing two pairs of AI smart glasses , one of which reportedly will not have cameras.
Screen-free AI devices are not entirely new, with products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend already attempting to bring AI assistants into standalone gadgets.

sources.title: The Nothing AI device is coming in December: No new screen, no app - Basic Tutorials
passages: The first Nothing AI device is set to ship as early as December 2026.
Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced this on November 4 in a lengthy essay titled “Toolmakers” on X.
There aren’t many details available yet beyond two key points: The device won’t feature a new screen, and, according to Pei, it couldn’t have been implemented as an app.
The name, price, specs, and a specific release date are still unknown.
Especially when it comes to data privacy for a device that’s supposed to be constantly listening, Nothing will have to explain very clearly in Europe where the recordings are processed.
Pei calls the device a tool, built with the personality and care that Nothing is known for.
Two details here are more interesting than they seem at first glance.
First, the word “new”: Pei doesn’t rule out that the device uses a screen—just not its own.
It stands to reason that your smartphone would take on this role, as Android Authority also points out.
Second, the word “ships”: Pei is talking about shipping, not just a December unveiling.
Whether this applies to Germany, however, remains to be seen.

OpenAI is working with Jony Ive on its own device without a traditional screen; according to Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon , several AI companies even plan to build their own smartphones; and in the smart glasses market, models like the XREAL Aura have long been driving change.
Nothing’s conclusion: first a productivity tool, then perhaps, at some point, the big consumer device.

extraction.body: The first Nothing AI device is set to ship as early as December 2026. Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced this on November 4 in a lengthy essay titled “Toolmakers” on X. There aren’t many details available yet beyond two key points: The device won’t feature a new screen, and, according to Pei, it couldn’t have been implemented as an app. The name, price, specs, and a specific release date are still unknown. The actual announcement comes at the very end of the essay, almost in passing. Pei calls the device a tool, built with the personality and care that Nothing is known for. The key sentence translates to: “It doesn’t have a new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Two details here are more interesting than they seem at first glance. First, the word “new”: Pei doesn’t rule out that the device uses a screen—just not its own. It stands to reason that your smartphone would take on this role, as Android Authority also points out. Second, the word “ships”: Pei is talking about shipping, not just a December unveiling. Whether this applies to Germany, however, remains to be seen. Most of the essay isn’t a product announcement, but rather a counterpoint to the industry. Pei takes a jab at the hunt for AI’s “iPhone moment”—that is, at the trackers, pins, glasses, and companion gadgets that many manufacturers are currently trying their luck with. He admires their courage but sees the situation differently. His argument goes like this: The iPhone was the culmination of decades of development, whereas AI is still in its infancy and stuck in the chat window. The models have long been powerful enough. What’s missing is context. Ideas from conversations and meetings rarely end up in writing anywhere, so AI knows little about your day. Nothing aims to close this “context gap.” Pei’s historical comparison fits well here: PCs and cell phones first gained traction in the workplace before making their way into living rooms. As an example, he cites the pager—which hung from the belts of doctors and anyone on call—as marking the beginning of mobile communication. Nothing’s conclusion: first a productivity tool, then perhaps, at some point, the big consumer device. Warning: this is where it gets speculative. Nothing hasn’t confirmed the form factor. However, the clues paint a fairly coherent picture: Anyone already familiar with Essential Space is currently using it on the Nothing Phone (3) , for example. A separate recording device that constantly listens in and provides context to the smartphone would be the logical hardware extension. Pei had already announced an AI-native device back in September 2025. At that time, Nothing raised $200 million in a Series C funding round led by Tiger Global, at a valuation of $1.3 billion. The first device was promised for 2026. Nothing is now just barely on track to meet that timeline. The road hasn’t been easy. This summer, Nothing confirmed a workforce reduction of about 40 percent while establishing its own “AI-native” business unit. At the same time, skyrocketing memory prices are taking a toll on affordable smartphones like the Nothing Phone (4b) . The AI device is therefore also a bet that Nothing won’t rely solely on the smartphone business in the future. The competition isn’t standing still. OpenAI is working with Jony Ive on its own device without a traditional screen; according to Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon , several AI companies even plan to build their own smartphones; and in the smart glasses market, models like the XREAL Aura have long been driving change. At the same time, the Humane Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 demonstrate just how quickly screenless AI gadgets can fail if they lack practical everyday utility. With “Toolmakers,” Pei skillfully steers clear of the hype trap. If you don’t promise an “AI iPhone,” you can’t fail by not delivering one. That’s a smart move in the wake of Humane’s disaster, and the lack of context is a real problem: Anyone who’s ever tried in vain to piece together the key points from memory after a meeting will immediately understand what Pei is getting at. My concern is different. If the Nothing AI device turns out to be nothing more than a stylishly designed voice recorder, Nothing will be entering a market that Plaud and others already occupy quite well. Then it won’t be the vision that matters, but rather, quite simply: price, transcription quality, data privacy, and whether the device works seamlessly with smartphones from other manufacturers. Especially when it comes to data privacy for a device that’s supposed to be constantly listening, Nothing will have to explain very clearly in Europe where the recordings are processed. We’ll know more in December. Basic Tutorials is a gaming and tech blog that keeps you up to date with in-depth news, reviews, tutorials and the latest deals from the world of gaming and technology. sources.title: Nothing teases its first AI device with no screen, launching in December
passages: London-based tech brand Nothing, famous for its striking transparent smartphones and audio gear, is gearing up to launch its very first AI device this December.

More details are expected to be revealed in the coming weeks ahead of the December launch.Taking on Amazon and the AI hardware rushNothing's entry into the AI hardware space comes at a time when major tech companies are rushing to release their own AI gadgets ahead of the holiday season, including new Alexa tablets from Amazon, as well as AI-focused hardware from Apple and Microsoft.Specifically, Nothing's reportedly recorder will step into a market where Amazon is already expanding its presence with its own AI-based voice recorders.Following its acquisition of the San Francisco-based startup Bee in July 2025 for an undisclosed sum, Amazon recently unveiled two new AI-powered listening devices designed to record, transcribe, and analyse conversations.The first is the Bee Frontier, a $75 wearable that can be worn on the wrist or clipped directly to clothing.

By confirming a screenless design, it is evident that users will interact with the device primarily through voice or other non-visual methods.Instead of making a general smart gadget for the home, Nothing is aiming this device squarely at professionals to boost workplace productivity.

Nothing CEO Carl Pei recently took to X (formerly Twitter) to confirm the timeline, dropping some major hints about the upcoming gadget.Interestingly, this new "AI-native" product will completely ditch the display and is being built as a dedicated hardware tool, rather than just another smartphone application.A screenless gadget built for the workplaceWhile the official name, exact launch date, and pricing are still a closely guarded secret, Pei’s teasers give buyers a clear picture of the company's direction.

extraction.body: The first Nothing AI device is set to ship as early as December 2026. Nothing CEO Carl Pei announced this on November 4 in a lengthy essay titled “Toolmakers” on X. There aren’t many details available yet beyond two key points: The device won’t feature a new screen, and, according to Pei, it couldn’t have been implemented as an app. The name, price, specs, and a specific release date are still unknown. The actual announcement comes at the very end of the essay, almost in passing. Pei calls the device a tool, built with the personality and care that Nothing is known for. The key sentence translates to: “It doesn’t have a new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Two details here are more interesting than they seem at first glance. First, the word “new”: Pei doesn’t rule out that the device uses a screen—just not its own. It stands to reason that your smartphone would take on this role, as Android Authority also points out. Second, the word “ships”: Pei is talking about shipping, not just a December unveiling. Whether this applies to Germany, however, remains to be seen. Most of the essay isn’t a product announcement, but rather a counterpoint to the industry. Pei takes a jab at the hunt for AI’s “iPhone moment”—that is, at the trackers, pins, glasses, and companion gadgets that many manufacturers are currently trying their luck with. He admires their courage but sees the situation differently. His argument goes like this: The iPhone was the culmination of decades of development, whereas AI is still in its infancy and stuck in the chat window. The models have long been powerful enough. What’s missing is context. Ideas from conversations and meetings rarely end up in writing anywhere, so AI knows little about your day. Nothing aims to close this “context gap.” Pei’s historical comparison fits well here: PCs and cell phones first gained traction in the workplace before making their way into living rooms. As an example, he cites the pager—which hung from the belts of doctors and anyone on call—as marking the beginning of mobile communication. Nothing’s conclusion: first a productivity tool, then perhaps, at some point, the big consumer device. Warning: this is where it gets speculative. Nothing hasn’t confirmed the form factor. However, the clues paint a fairly coherent picture: Anyone already familiar with Essential Space is currently using it on the Nothing Phone (3) , for example. A separate recording device that constantly listens in and provides context to the smartphone would be the logical hardware extension. Pei had already announced an AI-native device back in September 2025. At that time, Nothing raised $200 million in a Series C funding round led by Tiger Global, at a valuation of $1.3 billion. The first device was promised for 2026. Nothing is now just barely on track to meet that timeline. The road hasn’t been easy. This summer, Nothing confirmed a workforce reduction of about 40 percent while establishing its own “AI-native” business unit. At the same time, skyrocketing memory prices are taking a toll on affordable smartphones like the Nothing Phone (4b) . The AI device is therefore also a bet that Nothing won’t rely solely on the smartphone business in the future. The competition isn’t standing still. OpenAI is working with Jony Ive on its own device without a traditional screen; according to Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon , several AI companies even plan to build their own smartphones; and in the smart glasses market, models like the XREAL Aura have long been driving change. At the same time, the Humane Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 demonstrate just how quickly screenless AI gadgets can fail if they lack practical everyday utility. With “Toolmakers,” Pei skillfully steers clear of the hype trap. If you don’t promise an “AI iPhone,” you can’t fail by not delivering one. That’s a smart move in the wake of Humane’s disaster, and the lack of context is a real problem: Anyone who’s ever tried in vain to piece together the key points from memory after a meeting will immediately understand what Pei is getting at. My concern is different. If the Nothing AI device turns out to be nothing more than a stylishly designed voice recorder, Nothing will be entering a market that Plaud and others already occupy quite well. Then it won’t be the vision that matters, but rather, quite simply: price, transcription quality, data privacy, and whether the device works seamlessly with smartphones from other manufacturers. Especially when it comes to data privacy for a device that’s supposed to be constantly listening, Nothing will have to explain very clearly in Europe where the recordings are processed. We’ll know more in December. Basic Tutorials is a gaming and tech blog that keeps you up to date with in-depth news, reviews, tutorials and the latest deals from the world of gaming and technology. As an example, he cites the pager—which hung from the belts of doctors and anyone on call—as marking the beginning of mobile communication. Nothing’s conclusion: first a productivity tool, then perhaps, at some point, the big consumer device.
Warning: this is where it gets speculative. Nothing hasn’t confirmed the form factor. However, the clues paint a fairly coherent picture:

Anyone already familiar with Essential Space is currently using it on the Nothing Phone (3) , for example. A separate recording device that constantly listens in and provides context to the smartphone would be the logical hardware extension.

Pei had already announced an AI-native device back in September 2025. At that time, Nothing raised $200 million in a Series C funding round led by Tiger Global, at a valuation of $1.3 billion. The first device was promised for 2026. Nothing is now just barely on track to meet that timeline.

The road hasn’t been easy. This summer, Nothing confirmed a workforce reduction of about 40 percent while establishing its own “AI-native” business unit. At the same time, skyrocketing memory prices are taking a toll on affordable smartphones like the Nothing Phone (4b) . The AI device is therefore also a bet that Nothing won’t rely solely on the smartphone business in the future.

The competition isn’t standing still. OpenAI is working with Jony Ive on its own device without a traditional screen; according to Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon , several AI companies even plan to build their own smartphones; and in the smart glasses market, models like the XREAL Aura have long been driving change. At the same time, the Humane Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 demonstrate just how quickly screenless AI gadgets can fail if they lack practical everyday utility.

With “Toolmakers,” Pei skillfully steers clear of the hype trap. If you don’t promise an “AI iPhone,” you can’t fail by not delivering one. That’s a smart move in the wake of Humane’s disaster, and the lack of context is a real problem: Anyone who’s ever tried in vain to piece together the key points from memory after a meeting will immediately understand what Pei is getting at.

My concern is different. If the Nothing AI device turns out to be nothing more than a stylishly designed voice recorder, Nothing will be entering a market that Plaud and others already occupy quite well. Then it won’t be the vision that matters, but rather, quite simply: price, transcription quality, data privacy, and whether the device works seamlessly with smartphones from other manufacturers. Especially when it comes to data privacy for a device that’s supposed to be constantly listening, Nothing will have to explain very clearly in Europe where the recordings are processed. We’ll know more in December.

passages: London-based tech brand Nothing, famous for its striking transparent smartphones and audio gear, is gearing up to launch its very first AI device this December.

More details are expected to be revealed in the coming weeks ahead of the December launch.Taking on Amazon and the AI hardware rushNothing's entry into the AI hardware space comes at a time when major tech companies are rushing to release their own AI gadgets ahead of the holiday season, including new Alexa tablets from Amazon, as well as AI-focused hardware from Apple and Microsoft.Specifically, Nothing's reportedly recorder will step into a market where Amazon is already expanding its presence with its own AI-based voice recorders.Following its acquisition of the San Francisco-based startup Bee in July 2025 for an undisclosed sum, Amazon recently unveiled two new AI-powered listening devices designed to record, transcribe, and analyse conversations.The first is the Bee Frontier, a $75 wearable that can be worn on the wrist or clipped directly to clothing.

By confirming a screenless design, it is evident that users will interact with the device primarily through voice or other non-visual methods.Instead of making a general smart gadget for the home, Nothing is aiming this device squarely at professionals to boost workplace productivity.

extraction.body: China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says. The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Alice Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, isn't related to Jensen Huang.Who is Alice Huang?According to a 2025 New York Times report, Alice Huang has a scant online profile, but she has spent much of her career in China, which included working as a television reporter for Chinese state media.

Alice has reportedly also described herself as the firm's chief executive.What is she accused of?Citing people familiar with the matter, WSJ reported that authorities in Singapore, where Megaspeed is headquartered, and Taiwan have conducted separate investigations into Alice's China connections and deployed teams to monitor her movements.

With Huang's encouragement, Trump has reportedly enacted industry-friendly chip and AI policies, along with approving some sales of previous Nvidia chips to Beijing while negotiating with his counterpart Xi Jinping.In late 2024, officials from the US Commerce Department started investigating whether the Singapore-based Megaspeed was involved in diverting Nvidia's chips to China, bypassing Washington's export controls meant to protect crucial technologies.US security experts have raised concerns that companies may be bypassing restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips by setting up data centres in neighbouring countries and offering Chinese businesses remote access to their computing power.

Officials involved in the investigations suspected that Alice was recruited by intelligence agencies in Beijing after becoming aware of what they considered a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief.However, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs clarified on 31 October that neither the government nor its officials had expressed the concerns attributed to them in the WSJ report, and that no such investigations into Alice Huang’s alleged ties to Chinese intelligence had been conducted.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's reportedly close ties to a data-centre industry executive have now become a growing concern for officials in the US, Singapore and Taiwan. The executive is believed to be a Chinese intelligence source, possibly giving Beijing access to information about the world's most valuable artificial intelligence (AI) chips.According to The Wall Street Journal, in 2025, US officials concluded that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and top executive at Megaspeed International, passed information to the Chinese government while working with chipmaker Nvidia to build data centres in Asia. Alice Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, isn't related to Jensen Huang.Who is Alice Huang?According to a 2025 New York Times report, Alice Huang has a scant online profile, but she has spent much of her career in China, which included working as a television reporter for Chinese state media. According to a biography found on the social media of one of her former employers, she also worked as a private banker.She was also listed as a managing director for Megaspeed for its first eight months before she was removed from that role in its corporate paperwork. Alice has reportedly also described herself as the firm's chief executive.What is she accused of?Citing people familiar with the matter, WSJ reported that authorities in Singapore, where Megaspeed is headquartered, and Taiwan have conducted separate investigations into Alice's China connections and deployed teams to monitor her movements. Officials involved in the investigations suspected that Alice was recruited by intelligence agencies in Beijing after becoming aware of what they considered a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief.However, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs clarified on 31 October that neither the government nor its officials had expressed the concerns attributed to them in the WSJ report, and that no such investigations into Alice Huang’s alleged ties to Chinese intelligence had been conducted. It separately confirmed that investigations into Megaspeed were ongoing. In late 2024, when authorities began surveillance on Alice, she reportedly disappeared into Beijing for a while. Further, it can't be confirmed where she is now or whether she still holds a top executive role at Megaspeed.Chinese Embassy in US rejects allegationsWSJ reported that the Chinese Embassy in Washington rejected the allegations, saying that Beijing opposes what it described as the peddling of a "Chinese spy narrative" and adding that the country's technological development is grounded in "independent innovation."An Nvidia spokesperson said, "We’re confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," and added that CEO Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice "are not unusual or unexpected” given their business ties.A representative of the Singapore Police Force said investigations into Megaspeed were ongoing and declined to give specifics. “While we do not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, we act firmly against companies and individuals who violate our laws and are engaged in fraudulent and dishonest practices,” the representative said.Megaspeed probe and concerns over AI chip export loopholesChipmaker Nvidia's technology is said to be one of the most valued American technology assets, making its CEO a global superstar and helping him establish a close relationship with US President Donald Trump. With Huang's encouragement, Trump has reportedly enacted industry-friendly chip and AI policies, along with approving some sales of previous Nvidia chips to Beijing while negotiating with his counterpart Xi Jinping.In late 2024, officials from the US Commerce Department started investigating whether the Singapore-based Megaspeed was involved in diverting Nvidia's chips to China, bypassing Washington's export controls meant to protect crucial technologies.US security experts have raised concerns that companies may be bypassing restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips by setting up data centres in neighbouring countries and offering Chinese businesses remote access to their computing power. Analysts have also criticised the Trump administration for what they see as a reluctance to address these regulatory gaps.

sources.title: Spy targeting Nvidia CEO was alleged China intelligence service recruit: Report
passages: Washington DC: The Chinese businesswoman, with whom Nvidia's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Jensen Huang had alleged ties, was recruited as a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported, citing a memo circulated among policymakers in the Trump administration.On Friday, three House Republican committee chairs have asked Nvidia CEO to address, behind closed doors, the reported links with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of providing information to Beijing, Axios reported.Nvidia has denied the allegations as baseless .A top executive at a Singapore-based data centre firm named Megaspeed faced intense scrutiny over potential involvement in diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips towards China, as outlined in a report by The New York Times.

He also finalised a deal with Trump permitting the US government to secure a 25 per cent stake in specific Nvidia processors authorised for sale to China.As the Trump administration considered a comprehensive ban on Nvidia chip exports to China, Huang and his spouse travelled to Mar-a-Lago to persuade Trump to allow technology firms to continue doing business with Beijing.
As per the report, the Nvidia chief executive successfully lobbied the administration during Trump's second term to reverse stricter export controls governing the company's chip shipments to China.
I've always found Jensen Huang to be very aboveboard.

extraction.body: A senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed was under scrutiny over suspicions that she had helped divert advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. Now, according to a report by The New York Times, American intelligence officials have concluded that she was possibly a Chinese intelligence asset, passing information to Beijing. The investigation also revealed that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive. For years, Washington has sought to restrict China's access to the technology and expertise needed to match or surpass the United States in the intensifying global race for AI dominance. The possibility that Beijing may have gained information through someone with close ties to Jensen Huang, a central figure in the AI industry and an ally of US President Donald Trump, could raise further concerns in Washington. According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings, which had not previously been reported, but chose not to act. The report further states that American officials had already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade restrictions on its access to advanced AI chips. However, the assessment that she may have been passing information directly to Beijing has raised additional concerns. The situation is further complicated by Jensen Huang's reported access to Trump's thinking on an issue of critical importance to both countries, particularly as the US president prepares to visit China next month. Megaspeed said its “current leadership” was taking the matter “extremely seriously” and was committed to establishing the facts behind the allegations. Alice Huang's background Reporting by The New York Times has traced Alice Huang's rise from a Chinese businesswoman and investor to a senior executive at Megaspeed, a company that the US Commerce Department had begun scrutinising over suspicions that it was helping China evade American export restrictions and gain access to Nvidia's computing power. The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site suspicious. Nvidia equipment was still in its delivery packaging, raising concerns that the hardware might have been intended for onward shipment rather than installation at the facility. The US government has restricted exports of its most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022. While some firms have allegedly smuggled chips across the Chinese border, others have legally established businesses in Southeast Asia that purchase large quantities of chips to build data centres serving Chinese companies. Megaspeed has effectively operated as an intermediary, purchasing Nvidia chips through the American arm of Inspur. The parent company of Inspur had been blacklisted by the US government over allegations of supplying technology to the Chinese military. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia has also reportedly purchased advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between 2024 and February 2026. Nvidia is known to evaluate customers before selling them its chips and technology. Megaspeed has continued to appear on Nvidia's website, while a job advertisement from Megaspeed's Indonesian branch described the company as a “premier business partner of Nvidia”. Further questions have been raised about Alice Huang's background. She has maintained a limited public profile on the Chinese internet and has at times described herself as Megaspeed's chief executive, while the company has listed her as its managing director. She subsequently worked with several financial firms, including Hexi Capital. Media reports have also raised questions about how Megaspeed's executive used her connections to secure funding, promote the company's rapidly expanding network of businesses, pitch new projects, recruit employees and launch other initiatives. Megaspeed is also moving ahead with the construction of a major data centre in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new AI facilities have emerged amid palm oil plantations. The company has already secured the chips required for the project, adding another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding its access to advanced Nvidia hardware.

extraction.body: A senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed was under scrutiny over suspicions that she had helped divert advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. Now, according to a report by The New York Times, American intelligence officials have concluded that she was possibly a Chinese intelligence asset, passing information to Beijing. The investigation also revealed that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive. For years, Washington has sought to restrict China's access to the technology and expertise needed to match or surpass the United States in the intensifying global race for AI dominance. The possibility that Beijing may have gained information through someone with close ties to Jensen Huang, a central figure in the AI industry and an ally of US President Donald Trump, could raise further concerns in Washington. According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings, which had not previously been reported, but chose not to act. The report further states that American officials had already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade restrictions on its access to advanced AI chips. However, the assessment that she may have been passing information directly to Beijing has raised additional concerns. The situation is further complicated by Jensen Huang's reported access to Trump's thinking on an issue of critical importance to both countries, particularly as the US president prepares to visit China next month. Megaspeed said its “current leadership” was taking the matter “extremely seriously” and was committed to establishing the facts behind the allegations. Alice Huang's background Reporting by The New York Times has traced Alice Huang's rise from a Chinese businesswoman and investor to a senior executive at Megaspeed, a company that the US Commerce Department had begun scrutinising over suspicions that it was helping China evade American export restrictions and gain access to Nvidia's computing power. The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data centre in Malaysia and found the site suspicious. Nvidia equipment was still in its delivery packaging, raising concerns that the hardware might have been intended for onward shipment rather than installation at the facility. The US government has restricted exports of its most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022. While some firms have allegedly smuggled chips across the Chinese border, others have legally established businesses in Southeast Asia that purchase large quantities of chips to build data centres serving Chinese companies. Megaspeed has effectively operated as an intermediary, purchasing Nvidia chips through the American arm of Inspur. The parent company of Inspur had been blacklisted by the US government over allegations of supplying technology to the Chinese military. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia has also reportedly purchased advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between 2024 and February 2026. Nvidia is known to evaluate customers before selling them its chips and technology. Megaspeed has continued to appear on Nvidia's website, while a job advertisement from Megaspeed's Indonesian branch described the company as a “premier business partner of Nvidia”. Further questions have been raised about Alice Huang's background. She has maintained a limited public profile on the Chinese internet and has at times described herself as Megaspeed's chief executive, while the company has listed her as its managing director. She subsequently worked with several financial firms, including Hexi Capital. Media reports have also raised questions about how Megaspeed's executive used her connections to secure funding, promote the company's rapidly expanding network of businesses, pitch new projects, recruit employees and launch other initiatives. Megaspeed is also moving ahead with the construction of a major data centre in Johor, the Malaysian state across the border from Singapore, where new AI facilities have emerged amid palm oil plantations. The company has already secured the chips required for the project, adding another dimension to the scrutiny surrounding its access to advanced Nvidia hardware.

passages: TSMC rises on report of potential push into advanced memory for Nvidia
ADRs of TSMC surged 7.7% in early trading Friday as investors weighed the prospect of the foundry giant deepening its role in the critical AI hardware supply chain.

The Taiwanese manufacturer recently began formulating plans to produce vertically stacked 3D DRAM at the behest of its primary customer, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter cited by The Information.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The company's exploration is being spearheaded by Hsu Kuo-chin, a vice president directing TSMC's advanced packaging operations who previously ran Micron's regional footprint.

His oversight underscores how intimately memory architecture has become linked with advanced packaging, the specialized process required to tether memory and processing units into cohesive computing systems.
TSMC is examining whether to construct dedicated fabrication facilities or acquire and retool an existing site to support the specialized production, the report indicated.

That latter path mirrors a maneuver by Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU), which in March agreed to purchase a Taiwan-based facility from Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. for $1.8 billion to retrofit for high-end memory.
A persistent bottleneck in memory availability has driven hardware costs sharply higher, prompting key buyers such as Nvidia and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) to actively seek alternative procurement channels.
Apple, for its part, implemented price increases across its hardware portfolio earlier this year after absorbing substantial increases in memory procurement expenses.
Entering the memory arena would nonetheless expose TSMC to a notoriously volatile segment long dominated by Samsung Electronics (KS:005930), SK hynix Inc (NASDAQ:SKHY), and Micron.

Memory markets are historically prone to severe boom-and-bust supply imbalances, and while TSMC holds proprietary patents around vertical DRAM, translating lab designs into defect-free volume manufacturing poses formidable execution hurdles.

The strategic shift also introduces delicate competitive dynamics, particularly following TSMC's 2024 pact to manufacture base logic dies for SK Hynix's next-generation high-bandwidth memory products.

Entering the memory arena would nonetheless expose TSMC to a notoriously volatile segment long dominated by Samsung Electronics (KS:005930), SK hynix Inc (NASDAQ:SKHY), and Micron.

facts.text: TSMC rises on report of potential push into advanced memory for Nvidia
ADRs of TSMC surged 7.7% in early trading Friday as investors weighed the prospect of the foundry giant deepening its role in the critical AI hardware supply chain.

The Taiwanese manufacturer recently began formulating plans to produce vertically stacked 3D DRAM at the behest of its primary customer, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter cited by The Information.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The company's exploration is being spearheaded by Hsu Kuo-chin, a vice president directing TSMC's advanced packaging operations who previously ran Micron's regional footprint.

His oversight underscores how intimately memory architecture has become linked with advanced packaging, the specialized process required to tether memory and processing units into cohesive computing systems.
TSMC is examining whether to construct dedicated fabrication facilities or acquire and retool an existing site to support the specialized production, the report indicated.

That latter path mirrors a maneuver by Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU), which in March agreed to purchase a Taiwan-based facility from Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. for $1.8 billion to retrofit for high-end memory.
A persistent bottleneck in memory availability has driven hardware costs sharply higher, prompting key buyers such as Nvidia and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) to actively seek alternative procurement channels.
Apple, for its part, implemented price increases across its hardware portfolio earlier this year after absorbing substantial increases in memory procurement expenses.
Entering the memory arena would nonetheless expose TSMC to a notoriously volatile segment long dominated by Samsung Electronics (KS:005930), SK hynix Inc (NASDAQ:SKHY), and Micron.

Memory markets are historically prone to severe boom-and-bust supply imbalances, and while TSMC holds proprietary patents around vertical DRAM, translating lab designs into defect-free volume manufacturing poses formidable execution hurdles.

The strategic shift also introduces delicate competitive dynamics, particularly following TSMC's 2024 pact to manufacture base logic dies for SK Hynix's next-generation high-bandwidth memory products.

extraction.body: Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China. They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday. The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported. Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources. The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark. Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing. Nvidia instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different from his meetings with other executive clients. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. "China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. sources.title: Nvidia pushes back after Jensen Huang asked to closed-door meeting in Congress over ties to Chinese 'asset'
passages: Nvidia has pushed back after chief executive Jensen Huang was asked to appear before the US Congress to discuss his interactions with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

A representative for the powerful US-based AI and chip design company did not say whether Mr Huang would agree to attend the meeting with members of Congress, who requested his presence following reports that the Nvidia boss met with an executive of a Singapore company who is believed to have passed along information to China.

Republican Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Eric Crawford told the Nvidia boss in the letter that they have long been concerned about alleged Chinese espionage and the potential for it to result in the country getting access to “cutting-edge US technology”.
The House of Representatives select committee on the Chinese Communist Party had sent a letter to Mr Huang to request that he appear for a closed-door briefing.
“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security,” the Nvidia representative said.

Many Democrats across the country campaigned on trying to hold Big Tech executives more accountable, pushing for AI regulation and casting a critical eye on data centres – and all this might be bad news for Nvidia and Mr Huang.
Nvidia's push for relaxed export policies to China with regard to semiconductors has led to increased scrutiny in recent years.

Nvidia's push for relaxed export policies to China with regard to semiconductors has led to increased scrutiny in recent years. Company executives have insisted that strict export policies designed to improve the US lead over China in AI actually hurt the country and incentivise Beijing to use its own technology and develop in-house infrastructure. Critics say that by loosening export restrictions, the US is giving away its most important advantage to an adversary. The letter to Mr Huang was sent a day after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. Many Democrats across the country campaigned on trying to hold Big Tech executives more accountable, pushing for AI regulation and casting a critical eye on data centres – and all this might be bad news for Nvidia and Mr Huang. On Wednesday, Mr Blumenthal issued a notice to people, companies and government agencies that have “failed to co-operate” with a range of inquiries, including investigations into Big Tech and cryptocurrency. The notice said failure to produce requested records and information by January 4 would lead the committee to consider “alternative measures”. “Blumenthal is leading an inquiry into Big Tech companies and others who may be seeking pay-to-play government favours from their donations to President Trump’s White House ballroom and other projects,” a news release from Mr Blumenthal's office read. Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who will soon be in charge of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, was a bit more succinct following the midterms.

The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security,” the Nvidia representative said.
The House of Representatives select committee on the Chinese Communist Party had sent a letter to Mr Huang to request that he appear for a closed-door briefing.

Republican Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Eric Crawford told the Nvidia boss in the letter that they have long been concerned about alleged Chinese espionage and the potential for it to result in the country getting access to “cutting-edge US technology”.

“Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the letter concluded, asking for Mr Huang to appear and discuss his interactions with the alleged Chinese asset on November 18 behind closed doors.

The Nvidia representative told The National that the company has a robust security team that travels with its chief executive “when needed”, and that the company always acts accordingly when it receives updates from the US government about entities of concern.
“We're confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the representative added.
Mr Huang has become a familiar face in the halls of power in Washington over the past year, as he lobbied officials on US technology export policies.
Nvidia's push for relaxed export policies to China with regard to semiconductors has led to increased scrutiny in recent years.

Company executives have insisted that strict export policies designed to improve the US lead over China in AI actually hurt the country and incentivise Beijing to use its own technology and develop in-house infrastructure.
Critics say that by loosening export restrictions, the US is giving away its most important advantage to an adversary.
The letter to Mr Huang was sent a day after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Many Democrats across the country campaigned on trying to hold Big Tech executives more accountable, pushing for AI regulation and casting a critical eye on data centres – and all this might be bad news for Nvidia and Mr Huang.

On Wednesday, Mr Blumenthal issued a notice to people, companies and government agencies that have “failed to co-operate” with a range of inquiries, including investigations into Big Tech and cryptocurrency.
The notice said failure to produce requested records and information by January 4 would lead the committee to consider “alternative measures”.

“Blumenthal is leading an inquiry into Big Tech companies and others who may be seeking pay-to-play government favours from their donations to President Trump’s White House ballroom and other projects,” a news release from Mr Blumenthal's office read.
Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who will soon be in charge of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, was a bit more succinct following the midterms.

facts.text: Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday.
Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing.
The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to.
Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China.
"Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement.

President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported.
A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.
